These tags may trigger special effects and/or have values and meaning that can vary, even within the scope of a single play. Tags are additional parameters on top of the base meaning of the game element, so tags represent a means of coupling the game element with more mechanisms and systems. Tags are also bookmarks that can reference a variable set of possible rules that are encoded elsewhere, so tags are also a means to modularize, or uncouple, game triggers and game effects.


= = = = = = = = = =
In storytelling games, players are provided with conceptual, written, or pictorial stimuli which must be incorporated into a story of the players' creation. Once Upon a Time uses a selection of words while Rory's Story Cubes include ambiguous symbols. Some games like Snake Oil and Big Idea prompt players to pitch a product, which frequently takes the form of a brief story or vignette.

Other storytelling games include titles such as Tales of the Arabian Nights and Above and Below, game designs in which players don't create their own stories, but instead experience a story from the inside as one of the participants. Games along those lines might present players with a particular narrative situation, after which the player will make a choice that affects which end to the narrative is told — with the results of this narrative affecting the player's standing in the game.


= = = = = = = = = =
A game in which players are cooperating and competing with each other throughout the game, while trying to complete a common objective. To be classified as semi-cooperative, there must be two possible end states:

A) One or more (but unlikely to be all) players win
B) No players win

A game where players sometimes cooperate and sometimes compete but one always wins is not semi-cooperative. It is a Competitive game with a Negotiation mechanism.


= = = = = = = = = =
Secret unit deployment games are games that contain hidden information. Only the player controlling certain playing pieces has perfect information about the nature (or even the whereabouts) of those pieces. This mechanic is often used in wargames to simulate "fog of war".


= = = = = = = = = =
A game system that can be applied to a variety of different maps, starting resources and positions, and even different win and loss conditions. These variable conditions can be assembled into a broader narrative or campaign, or they can be entirely disconnected from one another.


= = = = = = = = = =
Some board games incorporate elements of role playing. It can be that players control a character that improves over time. It can also be a game that encourages or inspires Storytelling. This mechanic can be viewed as an extension of Variable Player Powers.


= = = = = = = = = =
Resources are generated from a random process and distributed to qualifying players.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players ask and answer questions in a manner constrained by rules.


= = = = = = = = = =
The Pieces themselves compose the Map.

This is distinct from Tile Placement in that the map elements remain “pieces” after placement, and accordingly continue to have agency in the game mechanics.


= = = = = = = = = =
Pieces are removed from a structure, and play is affected by things that fall (as in Ker Plunk), or a complete collapse of the structure (as in Jenga).


= = = = = = = = = =
Players possess one or more Action Tokens. Those who have an Action Token may take a turn, then they pass the token clockwise, allowing the next player to perform an action. Actions are performed in real time; - there is no pausing and structure within the turn.

Typically, to prevent stalling and to keep the game moving, in games with multiple Action Tokens, if both tokens are held by the same player, then they suffer a penalty.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players have a special ability that they can use one time per game.

These may be unique to them, like 'feats' in Warmachine, or common to all players, like the special power chits in Finca.

Often players will receive bonus Victory Points if they do not use their one-time abilities during the game.


= = = = = = = = = =
Actions, resources, or resolution are shared between neighbors.


= = = = = = = = = =
Multiple action options are presented to the players via a narrative format.

These can be presented in a book with numbered paragraphs as in Tales of the Arabian Nights or Above and Below, or via cards as in Dead of Winter: A Crossroads Game.


= = = = = = = = = =
Multiple actions are shown on a card, but only one can be used.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players Move Through a Deck of cards. Typically the goal is to reach the bottom (One Deck Dungeon), find and defeat a boss (Chainsaw Warrior), or simply know when to quit (Diamant).


= = = = = = = = = =
When a conflict is initiated, pieces are moved to a separate board for resolution.


= = = = = = = = = =
A set of cards in a specific relationship to one another that allows them to be played to a table or scored is a meld. When laying these cards down, the way the cards splay, or overlap one another, may sometimes reveal or conceal certain abilities or attributes.

Rummy games have players placing combinations of cards or tiles on the table to score. Innovation is a good example of the Splaying side, where players can spread cards out to show particular sets of icons to empower abilities.


= = = = = = = = = =
A set of cards in a specific relationship to one another that allows them to be played to a table or scored is a meld. When laying these cards down, the way the cards splay, or overlap one another, may sometimes reveal or conceal certain abilities or attributes.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players must make their next play by matching a feature on the previous play. This is frequently used in shedding games like UNO or Crazy Eights, where number or color/suit need to be matched.

In some implementations the next play needs to be in a number range based on the last. For example, in L.L.A.M.A. the play must be the same or one higher than the last. In Spit, it must be one higher or lower.

NOTE: Although this is similar to 'following suit' in a trick taking game, or 'ladder climbing' games, please use those mechanisms instead.


= = = = = = = = = =
Over the course of the game, the map shrinks.


= = = = = = = = = =
A multi-session game in which permanent and irreversible changes to the game state carry over to future plays. Components may be written on with permanent ink, torn apart, covered with a sticker, etc.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players contribute towards completing a task, but only the player who finally completes it gets a particular benefit or bonus reward (even if others share in the base level benefit).


= = = = = = = = = =
This is a meta-mechanic for Turn Order. Players may take an action that interrupts the normal turn flow.


= = = = = = = = = =
The number of Victory Points held by each player is private information.


= = = = = = = = = =
Movement occurs that is not visible to all players.

Scotland Yard is a classic game implementing this mechanism.

A key challenge for designers is determining how to make the movement rules simple enough that the players moving hidden units do not make mistakes, or that paths are traceable when the game concludes.


= = = = = = = = = =
Hand management games are games with cards in them that reward players for playing the cards in certain sequences or groups. The optimal sequence/grouping may vary, depending on board position, cards held and cards played by opponents. Managing your hand means gaining the most value out of available cards under given circumstances. Cards often have multiple uses in the game, further obfuscating an "optimal" sequence.

Hand management has no relationship to action/dexterity.


= = = = = = = = = =
Hand management games are games with cards in them that reward players for playing the cards in certain sequences or groups. The optimal sequence/grouping may vary, depending on board position, cards held and cards played by opponents. Managing your hand means gaining the most value out of available cards under given circumstances. Cards often have multiple uses in the game, further obfuscating an "optimal" sequence.


= = = = = = = = = =
When the main game ends, a special mini-game is played to determine the victor.


= = = = = = = = = =
Different Dice are used to move depending on unit or game state.


= = = = = = = = = =
"Dice Rolling" is a game mechanism that can be used for many things, randomness being the most obvious.

In wargames, "Dice Rolling" is used in conjunction with a variety of tables, notably a "Combat Results Table" (either as a Ratio or a Differential) which produces a result by strengths of both sides and a die roll (1D6, 2D6, and 1D10 are most commonly used).


= = = = = = = = = =
Players are trying to determine the identity of hidden information based on clues.
= = = = = = = = = =
Dice are rolled, and those exceeding a target number generate a success. Certain rolls (typically the highest and/or lowest on the die) generate additional success or extreme failure.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players coordinate their actions to achieve a common win condition or conditions. Players all win or lose the game together.


= = = = = = = = = =
Games may limit players from communicating with one another openly. These restrictions can be absolute as they relate to certain specific pieces of information, or they may restrict certain types of communication, such as speaking.

Examples of this mechanism include Hanabi and Reverse Charades.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players have a hand of cards that allows them to activate and perform actions with a subset of their units.


= = = = = = = = = =
Closed Drafting (or 'Card Drafting') is a means of distributing cards or other game elements to players through an ordered, closed selection process - typically "select and pass".

A typical implementation involves each player being dealt the same number of cards. Players then select one (or more) card(s) to keep, and pass the rest to their left. This continues until all cards are selected or discarded. 7 Wonders implements this type of draft.

An alternative is that only one player is dealt cards, and they take one and pass it until all players have cards. This obviously is strongly biased towards the first player, and needs to be supported thematically and balance-wise. Citadels implements this type of draft.

This is distinct from Open Drafting, with involves selection from a public display.


= = = = = = = = = =
Pieces are stationary but are built out in chains. This can give a dynamic sense of motion to the game, even though the pieces do not move.

Early examples of this mechanism can be found in Expedition and Through the Desert.


= = = = = = = = = =
Each player simultaneously or sequentially plays one or more cards. These modify the base outcome of a conflict and allow various special abilities to apply.

This can function similarly to Area Majority / Influence, but with a discrete resolution or award of the conflict target, rather than by dynamic/shifting control of a fixed asset. It is also similar to Force Commitment, but that mechanic presupposes a more liquid resource where the quantity can be chosen.


= = = = = = = = = =
Each player has a set of Actions available to them, embodied in cards, tokens, or some other affordance. Once performed, they are spent and may not be performed again until retrieved. Action Retrieval typically is itself an Action, or may take an entire turn.


= = = = = = = = = =
The earliest example of a game listed on Boardgamegeek that uses AP's is Special Train (1948).
= = = = = = = = = =
A player receives a number of Action Points or Operation Points on their turn. They may spend them on a variety of Actions.

The earliest example of a game listed on Boardgamegeek that uses AP's is Special Train (1948).

Economic games encourage players to manage a system of production, distribution, trade, and/or consumption of goods. The games usually simulate a market in some way. The term is often used interchangeably with resource management games.


= = = = = = = = = =
A strategy game is a game in which the players' decision-making skills have a high significance in determining the outcome. Strategy games often require decision tree analysis, or probabilistic estimation in the case of games with chance elements. Strategy games include abstract games, with artificial rules and little or no theme, and simulations (including wargames), with rules designed to emulate and reproduce a real or fictional scenario.

Voynich Game

Featuring real historical figures, realistic linguistics, archeological, botanical, geographical, historical, architectural and other game mechanics, deep lore—real and dramatized. Unfolding layers of gameplay, storytelling, and expansions.

If neither of your characters, historical or modern, are named/widely known… Then none of your cards can be, looked at by anyone, unless you choose to make them available,

Hidden mechanics:
Stereoscopic images that require two cards to be combined, sat next to each other correctly. The basic pack could have a stereoscopic viewer without any explanation, but sized just right to fit two cards.

Modifiable language cards to add your own language, with a little kit on how to linguistically build it out

VOYNICH GAME CANONICAL

The base game should be fairly light weight and accessible, but the more you play, the more mysteries are revealed, which adds layers to gameplay, and build into a much heavier weight game, or at least, the option to play it as a more heavyweight game. 

TRANSLATION 
As various translation proposals for words build up, the Maniscript Pool will evolve into what could be a sensible phrase, or could be nonsense. In order to be a successful translation, a manuscript language proposal must 1) match a majority (but need not match all) of the proposed glosses 2) must be built of the glosses proposed by being played on the manuscript pool words, and 3) must successfully win a consensus vote according to the voting rules in play. 

THE WIN DECK
If the players successfully translate the manuscript, they get to play a win round. There is a special deck just for this round, which operates as a reveal about the true nature of the manuscript. The core set comes with “The Order’s Secret Waterworks” win deck. The final round is only played with one or two cards per player, thus the reveal is surprising and mysterious with each game play, and depending upon how the win deck cards interact, there may be variable solutions to the mystery. However, many other win decks could be purchased as expansions with very different win game scenarios. 
Maybe—End Game scenarios are one of two things: Either somebody proves the manuscript is a hoax or gibberish, in which case they win and that’s the end of the game, or players arrive at a successful translation, revealing the existence of the win deck (maybe the win deck is hidden in the packaging with a win deck rulebook and not advertised, so it’s a really surprising reveal. The clues must be pieced together to come to the conclusion that the win deck even exists. The win deck rulebook should strongly request that players keep its existence secret. Perhaps some of the cards in the win deck could have codes which provide a discount on expansion packs? 


Lots of personality — characters, and game itself
There are “stock characters” and generated characters (based on attribute card randomization / name randomizing / setting, etc)

Lots of mystery and intrigue, hidden secret cards and rules and mechanics and characters. Out-of-game mechanics and legacy game mechanics…players may get to keep certain cards to be playable in future games. 

Actually… that might be the core:
You’ve got the manuscript pool
And you’ve got the character pool
The character pool is the character you’re dealing with in that round… they can help or harm, depending on your choices 

Card categories should have very clear and intuitive iconography… Like portrait frames for characters, parchment backgrounds for words and manuscript related stuff, other book like backgrounds

Mapping the manuscript to language…
Scrabble tiles that go on the word cards
Some sort of limited dictionary’s of a few languages maybe?
A little bit about language phrenology and morphology?

And card sourcing
Get lists of language features
Lists of botanicals
Constellations
Stars
Mabs
Kinds of castles
Medieval styles
Languages


Increase the number of character cards
And/or make composite built characters playable
We need Asian characters, New World characters
Seafaring characters
Different mystics and herbalists
Doctors
Alchemists
Royalls
Different academics
Linguists
Computer programmers
Soldiers


Other ideas
Maybe some characters players teams… Like a band of translators and soldiers who face the possibility of being eliminated during the war
Or the sisterhood/the order can be a team

VOYNICH GAME MECHANICS 

GENERAL OVERVIEW 
Players are working semi-privately on translating efforts
When they find a translation they think might be accepted by the scholarly community, they put their work into the public translation debate …a card with glyph chits and evidence on it(?) you may submit with up to one untranslated glyph, playing cards evidence with the word(s) makes it more likely that your translation will hold up later on

3	STANDARD ACTIONS [1 Backing chit unless otherwise specified]
	 - Propose a partial translation by playing a Gloss Card. If playing as your Character, play Gloss Card face-down on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Character Card. If playing as your Academic, play this card face up on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Academic card or any Voting Rules card in play. 
	 - You may propose an Alternate Manuscript language using a Language Card in your hand. This triggers a Scholarly Consensus Vote among all players with face-up Academic cards, according to the Voting Rules in play. Turn Gloss cards in the Manuscript common pool face down except those matching your proposed Manuscript Language. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card. 
	 - Propose a Crazy Idea Manuscript Language. You may also propose a novel suggestion for the Manuscript Language without playing a Language Card by spending 2 Backing chits.
	 - Propose a partial transliteration: Play a Glyph card on any Voynichese card in the Manuscript common pool. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card. 
	 - Play a card that changes the Voting Rules. Follow the instructions in the text printed on the card. 
	 - Flip your Character / Academic Card to change the play of your turn.
	 - Spend 2 Backing chits to flip your Character / Academic Card and change the play at any time during your turn.
	 - Contribute to the Manuscript lore by playing legend cards according to the rules on the card.
	 - Preserve one clue under a Preservation card in your Cache.
	UPKEEP
4	 - At the end of each turn, you must flip your Character / Academic card according to the instructions printed on it.
= = = = = = = = = =
Each author card counts as one Free Action when played in the final round. 			
= = = = = = = = = =
Each author card counts as one Free Action when played in the final round. 			
Voting:			
If you call a vote and your translation achieves Consensus, then you may take an extra turn [or draw an extra card?]. If Consensus fails, you lose your next turn [or discard?].			
= = = = = = = = = =
The Author Card: Each character has a corresponding Author Card. At the begining of a vote, the player who announces the vote draws a card. If you draw your author card, then you are the author of the manuscript, and you must look through the deck, removing all other Author cards from the deck. If any other card is drawn, you must look through the deck and choose seven(or whatever the number of characters is) cards of your choosing and place them face down in front of you. You may choose any cards in the deck, including any Author cards. These cards may not be used until the Final Round, in which they will replace your hand. You may not reveal the cards, nor whether or not you are the author (except by preserving evidence) until the end of the game. If you are the Author of the Manuscript, then begining with this vote, you MUST choose either to conceal your authorship by only voting against any Translation that indicates your authorship [e.g. votes that include any of Language(s) or Locality] or you must choose not to conceal your authorship by voting for any Translation that indicates your authorship. Once you have chosen whether or not to conceal your authorship, you may ONLY vote in accordance with this choice, you may not alternate. In either case, you may not reveal whether you are the author or not until the end of the game, except by preserving evidence.

Game objects, typically cards, have icons or other identifiers that identify them as belonging to specific categories. These tags may trigger special effects and/or have values and meaning that can vary, even within the scope of a single play. Tags are additional parameters on top of the base meaning of the game element, so tags represent a means of coupling the game element with more mechanisms and systems. Tags are also bookmarks that can reference a variable set of possible rules that are encoded elsewhere, so tags are also a means to modularize, or uncouple, game triggers and game effects.


= = = = = = = = = =
Game objects, typically cards, have icons or other identifiers that identify them as belonging to specific categories. These tags may trigger special effects and/or have values and meaning that can vary, even within the scope of a single play. Tags are additional parameters on top of the base meaning of the game element, so tags represent a means of coupling the game element with more mechanisms and systems. Tags are also bookmarks that can reference a variable set of possible rules that are encoded elsewhere, so tags are also a means to modularize, or uncouple, game triggers and game effects.


= = = = = = = = = =
In storytelling games, players are provided with conceptual, written, or pictorial stimuli which must be incorporated into a story of the players' creation. Once Upon a Time uses a selection of words while Rory's Story Cubes include ambiguous symbols. Some games like Snake Oil and Big Idea prompt players to pitch a product, which frequently takes the form of a brief story or vignette.

Other storytelling games include titles such as Tales of the Arabian Nights and Above and Below, game designs in which players don't create their own stories, but instead experience a story from the inside as one of the participants. Games along those lines might present players with a particular narrative situation, after which the player will make a choice that affects which end to the narrative is told — with the results of this narrative affecting the player's standing in the game.


= = = = = = = = = =
A game in which players are cooperating and competing with each other throughout the game, while trying to complete a common objective. To be classified as semi-cooperative, there must be two possible end states:

A) One or more (but unlikely to be all) players win
B) No players win

A game where players sometimes cooperate and sometimes compete but one always wins is not semi-cooperative. It is a Competitive game with a Negotiation mechanism.


= = = = = = = = = =
Secret unit deployment games are games that contain hidden information. Only the player controlling certain playing pieces has perfect information about the nature (or even the whereabouts) of those pieces. This mechanic is often used in wargames to simulate "fog of war".


= = = = = = = = = =
A game system that can be applied to a variety of different maps, starting resources and positions, and even different win and loss conditions. These variable conditions can be assembled into a broader narrative or campaign, or they can be entirely disconnected from one another.


= = = = = = = = = =
Some board games incorporate elements of role playing. It can be that players control a character that improves over time. It can also be a game that encourages or inspires Storytelling. This mechanic can be viewed as an extension of Variable Player Powers.


= = = = = = = = = =
Resources are generated from a random process and distributed to qualifying players.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players ask and answer questions in a manner constrained by rules.


= = = = = = = = = =
The Pieces themselves compose the Map.

This is distinct from Tile Placement in that the map elements remain “pieces” after placement, and accordingly continue to have agency in the game mechanics.


= = = = = = = = = =
Pieces are removed from a structure, and play is affected by things that fall (as in Ker Plunk), or a complete collapse of the structure (as in Jenga).


= = = = = = = = = =
Players possess one or more Action Tokens. Those who have an Action Token may take a turn, then they pass the token clockwise, allowing the next player to perform an action. Actions are performed in real time; - there is no pausing and structure within the turn.

Typically, to prevent stalling and to keep the game moving, in games with multiple Action Tokens, if both tokens are held by the same player, then they suffer a penalty.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players have a special ability that they can use one time per game.

These may be unique to them, like 'feats' in Warmachine, or common to all players, like the special power chits in Finca.

Often players will receive bonus Victory Points if they do not use their one-time abilities during the game.


= = = = = = = = = =
Actions, resources, or resolution are shared between neighbors.


= = = = = = = = = =
Multiple action options are presented to the players via a narrative format.

These can be presented in a book with numbered paragraphs as in Tales of the Arabian Nights or Above and Below, or via cards as in Dead of Winter: A Crossroads Game.


= = = = = = = = = =
Multiple actions are shown on a card, but only one can be used.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players Move Through a Deck of cards. Typically the goal is to reach the bottom (One Deck Dungeon), find and defeat a boss (Chainsaw Warrior), or simply know when to quit (Diamant).


= = = = = = = = = =
When a conflict is initiated, pieces are moved to a separate board for resolution.


= = = = = = = = = =
A set of cards in a specific relationship to one another that allows them to be played to a table or scored is a meld. When laying these cards down, the way the cards splay, or overlap one another, may sometimes reveal or conceal certain abilities or attributes.

Rummy games have players placing combinations of cards or tiles on the table to score. Innovation is a good example of the Splaying side, where players can spread cards out to show particular sets of icons to empower abilities.


= = = = = = = = = =
A set of cards in a specific relationship to one another that allows them to be played to a table or scored is a meld. When laying these cards down, the way the cards splay, or overlap one another, may sometimes reveal or conceal certain abilities or attributes.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players must make their next play by matching a feature on the previous play. This is frequently used in shedding games like UNO or Crazy Eights, where number or color/suit need to be matched.

In some implementations the next play needs to be in a number range based on the last. For example, in L.L.A.M.A. the play must be the same or one higher than the last. In Spit, it must be one higher or lower.

NOTE: Although this is similar to 'following suit' in a trick taking game, or 'ladder climbing' games, please use those mechanisms instead.


= = = = = = = = = =
Over the course of the game, the map shrinks.


= = = = = = = = = =
A multi-session game in which permanent and irreversible changes to the game state carry over to future plays. Components may be written on with permanent ink, torn apart, covered with a sticker, etc.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players contribute towards completing a task, but only the player who finally completes it gets a particular benefit or bonus reward (even if others share in the base level benefit).


= = = = = = = = = =
This is a meta-mechanic for Turn Order. Players may take an action that interrupts the normal turn flow.


= = = = = = = = = =
The number of Victory Points held by each player is private information.


= = = = = = = = = =
Movement occurs that is not visible to all players.

Scotland Yard is a classic game implementing this mechanism.

A key challenge for designers is determining how to make the movement rules simple enough that the players moving hidden units do not make mistakes, or that paths are traceable when the game concludes.


= = = = = = = = = =
Hand management games are games with cards in them that reward players for playing the cards in certain sequences or groups. The optimal sequence/grouping may vary, depending on board position, cards held and cards played by opponents. Managing your hand means gaining the most value out of available cards under given circumstances. Cards often have multiple uses in the game, further obfuscating an "optimal" sequence.

Hand management has no relationship to action/dexterity.


= = = = = = = = = =
Hand management games are games with cards in them that reward players for playing the cards in certain sequences or groups. The optimal sequence/grouping may vary, depending on board position, cards held and cards played by opponents. Managing your hand means gaining the most value out of available cards under given circumstances. Cards often have multiple uses in the game, further obfuscating an "optimal" sequence.


= = = = = = = = = =
When the main game ends, a special mini-game is played to determine the victor.


= = = = = = = = = =
Different Dice are used to move depending on unit or game state.


= = = = = = = = = =
"Dice Rolling" is a game mechanism that can be used for many things, randomness being the most obvious.

In wargames, "Dice Rolling" is used in conjunction with a variety of tables, notably a "Combat Results Table" (either as a Ratio or a Differential) which produces a result by strengths of both sides and a die roll (1D6, 2D6, and 1D10 are most commonly used).


= = = = = = = = = =
Players are trying to determine the identity of hidden information based on clues.
= = = = = = = = = =
Dice are rolled, and those exceeding a target number generate a success. Certain rolls (typically the highest and/or lowest on the die) generate additional success or extreme failure.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players coordinate their actions to achieve a common win condition or conditions. Players all win or lose the game together.


= = = = = = = = = =
Games may limit players from communicating with one another openly. These restrictions can be absolute as they relate to certain specific pieces of information, or they may restrict certain types of communication, such as speaking.

Examples of this mechanism include Hanabi and Reverse Charades.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players have a hand of cards that allows them to activate and perform actions with a subset of their units.


= = = = = = = = = =
Closed Drafting (or 'Card Drafting') is a means of distributing cards or other game elements to players through an ordered, closed selection process - typically "select and pass".

A typical implementation involves each player being dealt the same number of cards. Players then select one (or more) card(s) to keep, and pass the rest to their left. This continues until all cards are selected or discarded. 7 Wonders implements this type of draft.

An alternative is that only one player is dealt cards, and they take one and pass it until all players have cards. This obviously is strongly biased towards the first player, and needs to be supported thematically and balance-wise. Citadels implements this type of draft.

This is distinct from Open Drafting, with involves selection from a public display.


= = = = = = = = = =
Pieces are stationary but are built out in chains. This can give a dynamic sense of motion to the game, even though the pieces do not move.

Early examples of this mechanism can be found in Expedition and Through the Desert.


= = = = = = = = = =
Each player simultaneously or sequentially plays one or more cards. These modify the base outcome of a conflict and allow various special abilities to apply.

This can function similarly to Area Majority / Influence, but with a discrete resolution or award of the conflict target, rather than by dynamic/shifting control of a fixed asset. It is also similar to Force Commitment, but that mechanic presupposes a more liquid resource where the quantity can be chosen.


= = = = = = = = = =
Each player has a set of Actions available to them, embodied in cards, tokens, or some other affordance. Once performed, they are spent and may not be performed again until retrieved. Action Retrieval typically is itself an Action, or may take an entire turn.


= = = = = = = = = =
The earliest example of a game listed on Boardgamegeek that uses AP's is Special Train (1948).
= = = = = = = = = =
A player receives a number of Action Points or Operation Points on their turn. They may spend them on a variety of Actions.

The earliest example of a game listed on Boardgamegeek that uses AP's is Special Train (1948).

Economic games encourage players to manage a system of production, distribution, trade, and/or consumption of goods. The games usually simulate a market in some way. The term is often used interchangeably with resource management games.


= = = = = = = = = =
A strategy game is a game in which the players' decision-making skills have a high significance in determining the outcome. Strategy games often require decision tree analysis, or probabilistic estimation in the case of games with chance elements. Strategy games include abstract games, with artificial rules and little or no theme, and simulations (including wargames), with rules designed to emulate and reproduce a real or fictional scenario.

As various translation proposals for words build up, the Maniscript Pool will evolve into what could be a sensible phrase, or could be nonsense. Voynich game 

THE MANUSCRIPT can be played according to one of two Basic Game Styles: The standard Cross-Era Game included in the base set rulebook, and various Milieu Games which will consist of a mix-and-match combination of an Era Rule Book, and a Locale Rule Book. One Era-Locale pairing will be included in the Base Set, while others can be purchased as expansions. The two Basic Game Styles should have significantly different game play, using different rules and mechanics, and the many possible Era-Locale pairings will provide an even wider array of different moods and settings [Ideally, the Era and Locale rulebook distribution will be independently randomized so that different copies of the game will provide very different Milieu Game play style combinations]. The base set will also have some amount of hidden content that can be unlocked either through chance discovery, through gameplay easter eggs, or through company leaks / announcements. 
PLAYER INTRO Character Building Pool: When playing as your researcher, you may draw a card from the Character Pool. These cards are contact cards, which allow you to gain clues in areas of expertise other than your own. 
GAME STYLE: Each game is played in one of two Game Styles. Cross-Era Style is the default, played according to the BASE RULES below. Milieu Games are played according to the rules specified in the Era and Locale sections below. Game Style may be chosen according to any house rules the players agree upon. Alternately, you may use the following Optional Game Style Rules below. 
At the end of each round, anybody who drew a contact card that round flips over the card to reveal a partial character card. If there are two or more Character Building cards in the flip, then follow the rules on the cards to assemble a new characterin the Character Building Pool. This will be all players' guide to the next round, again using the text on the new Composit Character Card. Before the beginig of the next turn, be sure all players are informed of any rule changes made by the new Guide. 
OPTIONAL GAME STYLE RULES: If no player is carrying a Voynich Scholar Card, play an opening hand to determine the Game Style. The winner of the opening hand [see rules below] may choose either Cross-Era Style (standard rules) or Milieu Style. If Milieu Style is chosen, the game will proceed according to the rules of the Era and Locale of the opening hand winner. If any players are carrying Voynich Scholar cards, the Voynich Scholar with the most punched holes will choose whether to play standard Cross-Era Style or play a Milieu Style based on the opening hand rules. If two or more players carry Voynich Scholar cards with the same number of punched holes, then the player whose first name comes earliest in the alphabet must pick one player other than themselves to choose the Era and another to choose the Locale. 
The Author Card: Each character has a corresponding Author Card. At the begining of a vote, the player who announces the vote draws a card. If you draw your author card, then you are the author of the manuscript, and you must look through the deck, removing all other Author cards from the deck. If any other card is drawn, you must look through the deck and choose seven(or whatever the number of characters is) cards of your choosing and place them face down in front of you. You may choose any cards in the deck, including any Author cards. These cards may not be used until the Final Round, in which they will replace your hand. You may not reveal the cards, nor whether or not you are the author (except by preserving evidence) until the end of the game. If you are the Author of the Manuscript, then begining with this vote, you MUST choose either to conceal your authorship by only voting against any Translation that indicates your authorship [e. g. votes that include any of Language(s) or Locality] or you must choose not to conceal your authorship by voting for any Translation that indicates your authorship. Once you have chosen whether or not to conceal your authorship, you may ONLY vote in accordance with this choice, you may not alternate. In either case, you may not reveal whether you are the author or not until the end of the game, except by preserving evidence. 
The game comes with one rulebook for the basic Cross-Era Game, and one rulebook each for one of the Eras and one of the Locales included in the Base Set [Additional Era and Locale rules can be purchased as inexpensive expansions]. The Era and Locale rules combine to create a Milieu Game. 
If you draw an Author card at any other time, then you may keep it in your hand, discard. If that Author is in your Past [i.e. your left], then you may also choose to play it as a free action or Preserve it as evidence. Each author card counts as one Free Action when played in the final round. Voting: If you call a vote and your translation achieves Consensus, then you may take an extra turn [or draw an extra card?]. If Consensus fails, you lose your next turn [or discard?]. Each Character Has Different Goals: Wilfred: Translate & Sell BASE RULES (CROSS-ERA GAME) The Order: Endure & Be Heard - THE GOAL OF THE GAME: The basic INDIVIDUAL GOAL of all players is to propose as many PARTIAL TRANSLATIONS of THE MANUSCRIPT as they can in order to 
further the GROUP GOAL of successfully verifying a correct FULL TRANSLATION of the Manuscript, or... if the Manuscript turns out to be gibberish, by VERIFYING THE PERPETRATOR of the fraud. 
WWI: Translate & Survive - GAME PLAY: The Manuscript is built from untranslated VOYNICHESE cards played face up in the COMMON POOL. When all Voynichese cards in the common pool are translated, the game is won and the player who proposed the translation wins. The player with the most clout chits is the second runner up (the winner could also be the second runner up). The second runner up from a game gets to keep a Voynich Scholar card [A pack of Voynich Scholar cards comes with the starter set, along with a hole punch to mark wins]. A player carrying the Voynich Scholar card with the most punches gets to choose the style / era of game play. Ties are determined through a die-roll. If there are no players carrying Voynich Scholar cards, then style of game play is chosen by consensus or die roll. 
Internet Researcher: Translate & Gain Clout - To do this, players PROPOSE partial translations by laying GLOSS cards on the Manuscript as it appears in the COMMON POOL in the center of the table. The process of translation is helped by gaining various forms of BACKING to allow more actions during your turn. The translation process can also be helped (or hindered!) as the players come to CONSENSUS over the PROVENANCE (source) of the manuscript and then come to consensus over the TRANSLATION OF THE MANUSCRIPT. The game is won by successfully VERIFYING the provenance, language, and translation of the manuscript. 
The Alchemist: - Game play proceeds as players use cards from their hand to propose PARTIAL TRANSLATIONS, to propose various PROVENANCES and LANGUAGE HYPOTHESES. When a player proposes a partial (or full) translation, provenance, or language hypothesis, the players vote on consensus according to the VOTING RULES in play. If consensus is reached, it makes the translation based on that provenance or language easier to proceed. If consensus is not reached, then translations based on all proposed provenances and languages are equally easy to proceed with, but only one can be correct in the end [usually!]. Translation is further helped along by VERIFYING THE PROVENANCE and eventually VERIFYING THE TRANSLATION of The Manuscript. However -- the Manuscript may turn out to be a gibberish fraud, in which case, VERIFYING THE TRANSLATION requires succesfully VERIFYING THE PERPETRATOR of the fraud. 
Rudolph: 
GAME START - Players choose their characters or are assigned by chance draw at the begining of the game. Each character also has an associated member of the academic community printed on the reverse. During their turn players may play as either their character or the member of the academic community on the back of their player card by flipping the character card to show which they are playing as. Which role you play during your turn will be determined by various effects printed on cards. - Players sit from left to right according to their era -- earliest to latest. Unless otherwise specified, each hand always begins with the same person throughout the duration of the game player playing the earliest character. - Each character is associated with particular era(s) and/or manuscript provenance (based on location, linguistic, and other clue cards) and language(s). - All players to your left are past characters, all players to your right are future characters. - The GROUP GOAL is to establish which provenance is the true origin of the manuscript, and then to translate it in accordance with the language(s) associated with that provenance. BASIC GAME PLAY - When you are playing as your academic, you are considered to be playing in the present, otherwise all characters are considered to be in the past of both the academic community, and all players to their left. When you are playing as your character, you are considered to be in the past of all players to your right and in the future of all players to your left. Likewise, all players to your left are in your past and all players to your right are in your future. - Voynichese cards printed with an untranslated word from the manuscript are played immediately into the body of knowledge to be translated by group effort. - Players collect glyph and gloss cards to unlock the meanings of different Voynichese cards. - Glyph cards are transliterations of individual letters of Voynichese, while gloss cards are translations of full words. There are a total of 8114 different Word cards, but only a certain [randomized?] set of them will be packaged with the Starter Set. Additional word packs may be purchased. The more word cards you have, the more varied the possible translations. Players may bring up to three of their own Word cards, which can be played into the Manuscript Pool in exchange for up to three bonus actions, but only in the first hand. Any Word cards played in this way become property of that set's owner. All word cards must be played immediately, regardless of their origin, unless specified otherwise on a card in play [e.g. a card played by a player, face up on the table as an action or in a character's Cache.] - All translations are considered tentative until player consensus (or sufficient evidence) "locks in" the first verified translation, thereby determining the language (and provenance) of the manuscript. Multiple translation attempts may be in play at any given time. HOWEVER -- player consensus may turn out to be wrong (provenance / translations supported by evidence may also be wrong, until sufficient evidence is gathered to "prove" its veracity). - Players further their individual translation efforts by gaining Backing through grants / patronage / clout by either "announcing" a translation or via various effects printed on cards. - The more backing you have, the more you can do on your turn. Backing is tracked with chits, and you may take as many actions during your turn as you have backing chits, unless otherwise specified on various cards. - Any player with their academic card face up may announce a manuscript language hypothesis and/or a proposed translation at any time using an announcement card, but they will only gain clout if the academic community (all players with their academic card up) agrees -- voting will proceed immediately upon announcement of a proposed translation (normal voting proceeds by black / white bean count or show of hands, but voting rules can be changed using effects printed on various cards). Players decide for themselves how to vote based on whether the announced translation sounds real or like gibberish, but once a consensus is made, only translation cards using the announced language will be considered free actions, all other translation cards must be played at a cost -- either clout / backing chits or using effects printed on cards. - Consensus makes it easier to proceed with translations in accordance with the proposed provenance and language voted on in the consensus vote by making cards with the current consensus translation / provenance free actions. - Once the manuscript language is verified, only translations and clues associated with that language / provenance will be playable. - Some types of cards can be passed (successfully or unsuccessfully) from past players to future players using preservation cards. - Words, glyphs, artifacts, legends and some other cards may be passed according to the rules on the cards. - You may pass cards by "preserving" them in your cachet (in front of you) by playing them under a preservation card. - Future players can unlock any past player's preserved cards using "clue" cards. - Players may also search the discard stack for past preservation cards -- search the top [die roll] cards, if you find a preservation card, you may search [die roll] cards under that preservation card, and keep any that match the preservation method. - Glyphs and glosses may be preserved with any preservation method unless otherwise specified. - Botanical cards may be preserved with amphorae, tomes, or horticulture cards. 
YOUR TURN 1 EXPAND THE POOL 
You must always play any Voynichese card in your hand into the Manuscript common pool. Placing a Voynichese card into the Manuscript common pool always counts as a free action and MUST be done as soon as it is drawn, ragardless of whose turn it is unless otherwise specified by text printed on a card in play. 
2 FREE ACTIONS
- You may draw one card from the deck per turn as a free action, or spend Backing chits to draw additional cards. - You may take any number of other free actions, as specified above, or as instructed by text printed on various cards in play. - You may play one card from your hand or from your Cache according to the instructions printed on the card. - You may take a number of actions equal to the number of Backing chits you have, or according to the Backing cost printed on the card. 
- Propose a Manuscript Language from any of the languages currently in play (as specified by text on all face-up cards anywhere on the table). - You may discard any number of cards from your hand or your Cache. If you choose to discard a Preservation card, then you must also discard any evidence you have preserved underneath it. 
3 STANDARD ACTIONS [1 Backing chit unless otherwise specified] - Propose a partial translation by playing a Gloss Card. If playing as your Character, play Gloss Card face-down on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Character Card. If playing as your Academic, play this card face up on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Academic card or any Voting Rules card in play. - You may propose an Alternate Manuscript language using a Language Card in your hand. This triggers a Scholarly Consensus Vote among all players with face-up Academic cards, according to the Voting Rules in play. Turn Gloss cards in the Manuscript common pool face down except those matching your proposed Manuscript Language. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card. - Propose a Crazy Idea Manuscript Language. You may also propose a novel suggestion for the Manuscript Language without playing a Language Card by spending 2 Backing chits. - Propose a partial transliteration: Play a Glyph card on any Voynichese card in the Manuscript common pool. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card. - Play a card that changes the Voting Rules. Follow the instructions in the text printed on the card. - Flip your Character / Academic Card to change the play of your turn. - Spend 2 Backing chits to flip your Character / Academic Card and change the play at any time during your turn. - Contribute to the Manuscript lore by playing legend cards according to the rules on the card. - Preserve one clue under a Preservation card in your Cache. 
UPKEEP 4 - At the end of each turn, you must flip your Character / Academic card according to the instructions printed on it. 
EXAMPLE ERA-BASED GAME RULES

I think this game idea is extremely strong—it’s ambitious, original, and has a lot of layers that could make it stand out in the tabletop space. A few highlights:  

**What’s working really well**  
- **The theme is gold.** Using the real-world mystery of the Voynich Manuscript as the backbone makes the game instantly intriguing, and the idea of “deciphering” through consensus rather than finding a real solution is brilliant【14†source】.  
- **The mechanics fit the theme.** Transliteration (Glyphs), translation (Gloss), and peer review (Consensus votes) map neatly to academic research, while hidden roles (the Author mechanic) mirror the hoax/real manuscript debate【16†source】【17†source】.  
- **Replayability is built in.** Between Cross-Era and Milieu play styles, randomized rulebooks, and hidden content (blacklight ink, stereoscopic images, “win decks”), no two games would feel the same【14†source】【18†source】【19†source】.  
- **Asymmetric characters.** Playing historical figures (Kircher, Dee, Voynich, Friedman, even modern conspiracy theorists) with unique goals ensures varied strategies and roleplay flavor【14†source】【20†source】.  
- **Meta-game design.** The inclusion of secret expansions and hidden rules that players might discover in real life echoes the mystique of the manuscript itself, encouraging a cult following【14†source】【21†source】.  

**Potential challenges**  
- **Complexity curve.** There’s a *lot* going on—translation layers, dual-sided roles, era-based seating, preservation caches, and secret win decks. It’s immersive, but could overwhelm casual players. The design documents do mention starting light and layering in depth over time, which is the right approach【19†source】【21†source】.  
- **Balance of cooperation vs competition.** Since it’s semi-cooperative, there’s a risk of “kingmaking” or players feeling like their contributions don’t matter if someone else seizes consensus. Careful balancing of Clout/Backing rewards will be key【16†source】【17†source】.  
- **Production costs.** Features like blacklight ink, stereoscopic cards, randomized rulebooks, and modular expansions are awesome, but also expensive to manufacture and could complicate retail distribution.  

**Why it’s exciting**  
It’s not just a puzzle game or a deduction game—it’s a game about how humans make meaning when faced with the unknowable. That’s clever and unique, and if the mechanics are streamlined just enough to keep it playable, I could see this becoming a cult classic in the same vein as Arkham Horror or Sherlock Holmes Consulting Detective.  

👉 Overall: I think the concept is brilliant and thematically perfect. The next step would be to refine *how much* of the complexity to include in the base game versus expansions, so it feels approachable but still has the “deep rabbit hole” vibe that matches the Voynich Manuscript.  

Would you like me to put together a **playtest-ready “lite version” ruleset** (a stripped-down core loop with the essential mechanics), so you can test it with players before layering on all the hidden content?

The Voynich Game: System Specification Document
1.0 Game Overview & Core Vision
This document details the complete mechanical and systematic framework for The Voynich Game, a tabletop experience centered on the collaborative and competitive decipherment of the world's most mysterious manuscript. The game's design is engineered to marry deep thematic immersion—drawing from the real-world history, figures, and academic debates surrounding the Voynich Manuscript—with a robust strategic gameplay engine. Players will navigate centuries of scholarly intrigue, forming and breaking alliances to either uncover a profound historical truth or expose a masterful fraud.
The high-level specifications of the game are as follows:
	•	Game Concept: To collectively and competitively decipher the Voynich Manuscript by proposing and verifying translations, establishing foundational hypotheses, and voting on the validity of scholarly claims.
	•	Player Dynamics: A unique blend of collaborative research, where players build upon each other's work, and competitive, secret-driven goals, where individual ambitions and hidden roles can shift the course of history.
	•	Core Engine: A card-based system driven by linguistic logic, the strategic preservation and transfer of information across historical eras, and a central social deduction mechanic based on achieving scholarly consensus.
	•	Winning the Game: Victory is achieved by reaching one of two end-states: either a player or group achieves a verified full translation of the manuscript through the Consensus & Voting system, or a player successfully identifies the perpetrator of a fraud, as determined by the secret Author Card mechanic.
These specifications are built upon a set of foundational concepts that serve as the pillars of the gameplay experience.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2.0 Foundational Game Concepts
This section breaks down the key conceptual pillars that define the strategic landscape of The Voynich Game. A firm grasp of these concepts is crucial for understanding the intricate interplay between players, their resources, and their interaction with the game's central, enigmatic puzzle.
The Manuscript Pool The Manuscript Pool is the shared central play area where all untranslated Voynichese Word Cards are played. This pool represents the collective body of knowledge about the manuscript itself, forming the evolving puzzle that all players are working to solve. Actions taken by players will primarily target or build upon the cards within this pool.
Clout & Backing These are the two primary resources players manage. Clout is a measure of academic prestige, reputation, and influence within the scholarly community; it is often gained through successful proposals or specific card effects. Backing represents institutional support, funding, and the general capacity to perform work. It is spent in the form of chits, with each chit typically funding one standard action. The more Backing a player has, the more they can accomplish on their turn.
Consensus & Voting This is the central social mechanic of the game. When a player proposes a significant translation or a major hypothesis, a vote is triggered among the players. Achieving "Consensus" is a powerful event; it can grant the proposing player rewards and makes all future actions related to that hypothesis significantly easier, often converting them into free actions for all players. This system simulates the process of peer review and the formation of academic paradigms.
Provenance & Hypotheses These represent the two main theories that players work to establish. Provenance is a hypothesis about the origin, or source, of the manuscript. Language Hypotheses are theories about the specific language the manuscript is written in or the cipher used to encode it. Establishing consensus on these foundational theories is a critical step toward a successful translation.
Eras & Chronological Play The game is structured chronologically. Each player embodies a character from a specific historical period, and players are seated in order from the earliest era to the latest. This seating order affects the flow of information; players in the "past" (to the left) can use Preservation cards to save clues and translations for players in the "future" (to the right) to discover, simulating the passage of knowledge through time.
Dual Player Roles (Character & Academic) Each player card is two-sided, representing a dual role. The Characterside represents a specific historical persona with unique goals and abilities. The Academic side represents their modern scholarly counterpart. This system is designed to create a core strategic tension; players must choose whether to engage with the manuscript's historical context directly (as the Character) or to engage with the meta-puzzle of academic theory and peer review (as the Academic). Flipping their card during a turn is a strategic choice to access different sets of actions, reflecting the distinction between direct historical action and modern scholarly analysis.
These core concepts are brought to life through the game's primary components: the card ecosystem.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3.0 Game Components: The Card Ecosystem
The cards are the primary engine of The Voynich Game, driving every action from proposing a simple transliteration to altering the fundamental rules of play. This section provides a comprehensive catalog of all card types, analyzing how each one contributes to the game's mechanical depth and thematic narrative.
Card Type	Core Function	Example(s)
Word Card	The central puzzle pieces. Untranslated Voynichese words that are played into the Manuscript Pool to be decoded.	fchorchdy
Glyph Chit	Proposes a transliteration for a single Voynichese symbol. The foundational layer of translation.	“𐑒 = K”
Gloss Card	Proposes a full word translation, building upon Glyph transliterations. The primary tool for solving the puzzle.	“fchorchdy = ‘sacred salve’”; "Old High German: WERALT : WORLD"
Proposal Card	Puts forth a major theory about the manuscript's origin (Provenance) or language. Used to establish a consensus.	“Proposal: Language = Old High German”
Preservation Card	Allows a player to store (cache) other cards (like Gloss or Clue cards) for later use or for future players to find. Introduces strategic planning and information hiding.	Amphora, Tome
Evidence Card	Supports or refutes a hypothesis or translation, adding weight to votes and building a case for a specific theory.	“Alder Pollen”, “Pollen Match: Strong match with 15th century Bohemian flora”
Investigation Card	Grants special actions related to discovery, such as searching discard piles or gaining clout from a specific field of study.	Cryptography, Unknown Botanical Sample, Palynology
Contact Card	Allows a player to gain clues or access knowledge from fields of study outside their character's expertise, adding strategic flexibility.	“Contact: Forensic Botanist”
Character Card	Defines the player's asymmetric historical persona, including their unique goals, abilities, and era.	Wilfrid Voynich, Athanasius Kircher
Author Card	A secret role card. If drawn, that player is secretly the manuscript's author, introducing a hidden traitor/bluffing mechanic with specific voting restrictions.	Author Card Wilfrid Voynich
Backing Card	Grants resources, typically Clout chits or extra actions, representing institutional support or academic funding.	“Grant: The British Museum will fund 2 extra actions...”
Voting Rules Card	A card that temporarily or permanently alters the rules for how consensus votes are conducted.	“Rule Change”
Page Card	Thematic cards that provide a free action if their subject (e.g., Herbal, Cosmological) is the dominant evidence type in the Manuscript Pool.	Pharmaceutical, Herbal, Cosmological
Fragment Card	A minor thematic component, often played for a free, small effect that contributes to the overall puzzle.	Manuscript Fragment
Era/Locale Rule Card	Defines specific rules, tools, and worldviews for a given historical period or setting in Milieu-style games.	“Renaissance – Alchemy permitted as valid evidence...”
The following section will detail how these components are arranged to begin a game.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.0 Game Setup & Structure
The setup phase is critical, as it establishes the game's style, assigns player roles, and constructs the chronological framework that will govern the flow of play and information throughout the session.
	1.	Choose Game Style: Before the game begins, players must select one of two styles. The decision is typically made by the player holding a Voynich Scholar Card with the most marks; otherwise, it is determined by an opening hand or consensus.
	•	Cross-Era Game: This is the standard style, played according to the base rulebook, featuring characters from disparate historical periods interacting across time.
	•	Milieu Game: This style uses a specific Era Rule Book and Locale Rule Book to create a more focused and thematic setting, with unique rules and mechanics tailored to that specific time and place.
	2.	Assign Characters: Each player chooses or is randomly assigned a Character Card. This card dictates their historical persona, special abilities, and potential victory conditions for the game.
	3.	Establish Seating Order: Players arrange themselves at the table chronologically, from left to right, according to their character's historical era (e.g., a 15th-century character sits to the left of a 17th-century character). For gameplay purposes, players to one's left are considered to be in the "past," while players to one's right are in the "future."
	4.	Prepare Decks and Pools: The central Manuscript common pool area is cleared, and the main deck of cards is shuffled. Players are dealt their starting hands according to the rules of the chosen game style.
With the historical stage set, the game begins its dynamic progression through the ages.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.0 Gameplay Flow: A Round in Detail
A round in The Voynich Game is a chronological progression of turns, moving from the earliest era player to the latest. Each player takes actions that can have cascading effects, as a discovery or theory proposed in one era can influence the options and information available to players in subsequent eras. For example, Sir Francis Bacon (early 1600s) might propose a theory that Athanasius Kircher (mid-1600s) can then build upon, while Wilfrid Voynich (early 1900s) may "preserve" a key clue that a 21st-century theorist can later unearth.
An individual player's turn is structured into the following phases:
	1.	Expand the Pool This is a mandatory free action. If the card drawn during the "Draw one card" free action is a Voynichese Word Card, it must be played immediately into the Manuscript Pool, expanding the collective puzzle for everyone.
	2.	Take Actions A player may take a number of actions based on their available resources, primarily Backing chits. Actions are divided into two types:
	•	Free Actions: These do not cost Backing and can be performed as specified.
	•	Draw one card from the deck.
	•	Play any card that has been designated as a free action (e.g., through a previously established consensus).
	•	Play one card from their personal cache if enabled by a Preservation card's effect.
	•	Standard Actions (Cost: 1 Backing Chit): These are the core strategic moves a player can make by spending one Backing chit per action.
	•	Propose a full word translation by playing a Gloss Card.
	•	Propose a single-symbol transliteration by playing a Glyph Chit.
	•	Play a Rule Change card to alter the voting mechanics.
	•	Flip their Character/Academic Card to switch roles and access different abilities.
	•	Preserve a clue by playing a card from their hand into their personal cache under a Preservation card.
	3.	Upkeep In the final phase of a turn, players perform any necessary cleanup. This may include flipping their Character/Academic card back to its default side as per card instructions or other end-of-turn effects.
This turn structure provides the framework for the game's most critical and interactive mechanical systems.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.0 Core Mechanics Deep Dive
Mastery of The Voynich Game requires a deep understanding of its pivotal systems. This section provides a detailed codification of the game's most crucial mechanics, outlining their rules and strategic implications.
The Translation Process Translation is a two-layered process that forms the game's central puzzle.
	1.	First, players propose transliterations for individual Voynichese symbols by playing Glyph Chits onto Word Cardsin the Manuscript Pool. This establishes a foundational "alphabet" for a given word.
	2.	Next, players can propose a full word translation by playing a Gloss Card. For a Gloss Card to be successful, it should align with previously accepted Glyph Chits. As a strategic incentive for collaboration, whenever a Gloss Card is successfully played using another player's glyph, the originator of that Glyph Chit is rewarded with Backing chits.
The Consensus & Voting System Voting is triggered whenever a player proposes a major translation or a foundational hypothesis (such as the manuscript's language or provenance). The outcome of the vote has significant consequences:
	•	Consensus Achieved: If the proposal gains consensus (e.g., via majority vote), the proposer may be rewarded with an extra turn. More importantly, actions related to the newly accepted hypothesis (such as playing Gloss Cards in the consensus language) become easier, often becoming free actions for all players.
	•	Consensus Fails: If the proposal is voted down, the proposer faces a penalty, such as losing their next turn. This mechanic forces players to carefully consider when to put forth a theory and to lobby for support from their peers.
Preservation & Information Transfer This mechanic allows for the strategic management and transfer of information across time. Using Preservation Cards like an Amphora or Tome, a player can create a personal Cache in front of them.
	•	Placing Cards: A player can spend an action to place cards (such as valuable Gloss or Clue cards) from their hand into their Cache.
	•	Sealing: Some Preservation cards can be "Sealed," protecting the information within but preventing further additions.
	•	Retrieval: A player in a "future" era can use Clue Cards to retrieve information from a "past" player's preserved cache, simulating the rediscovery of lost knowledge and creating opportunities for long-term strategic planning.
The Author Mechanic This is a secret role mechanic that introduces an element of bluffing and hidden identity.
	•	Discovery: A player discovers they are the Author by drawing their own character's Author Card during a specific game event (e.g., when calling a vote). Upon doing so, they must secretly search the deck and remove all other Author Cards from the game.
	•	The Critical Choice: The Author must immediately make a binding choice: they will either consistently vote against any theory that points to their true identity (concealing it), or they will consistently vote for such theories (revealing it). They cannot alternate between these strategies.
	•	Final Round: The Author secretly sets aside a special hand of seven cards, which replaces their normal hand during the game's Final Round, giving them a powerful, hidden advantage in the endgame.
These mechanics find their most unique expression through the game's diverse and asymmetric cast of characters.
