Marketing Proposal: The Voynich Game
1.0 Introduction: The Unsolved Mystery as a Market Opportunity
For centuries, the Voynich Manuscript has remained one of history's most compelling and unyielding enigmas—a book written in an unknown script by an unknown author, filled with illustrations of unidentifiable plants and cryptic diagrams. This real-world mystery is more than a historical curiosity; it is a powerful, untapped narrative engine, perfectly suited for an immersive tabletop experience that challenges players to do what centuries of scholars could not: unravel its secrets.
This proposal introduces The Voynich Game, a strategically deep and thematically rich game designed to capture the academic rivalries, collaborative breakthroughs, and deceptive dead-ends of the global effort to decipher the manuscript. Our objective is to outline the game's unique design, its significant potential for commercial success, and its inherent capacity for fostering passionate community engagement.
We will now detail how The Voynich Game translates this historical intrigue into a compelling and unforgettable core gameplay experience.
2.0 The Core Experience: Decipher, Deceive, and Discover
The strategic heart of The Voynich Game is its core gameplay loop, a system meticulously designed to simulate the real-world dynamics of academic research. It is an environment of intense competition and fragile alliances, where players must navigate scholarly disputes, forge consensus, and guard against misinformation in a shared quest for the truth. This loop transforms the solitary act of deciphering a text into a dynamic social and strategic challenge.
The game's central actions are designed to be intuitive yet layered, creating a cycle of proposal, debate, and discovery:
	•	Confront the Manuscript: Players begin by drawing and playing Voynichese Word cards into a shared pool, creating the central, unsolved text that the group must collectively decipher.
	•	Propose Meanings: Players use Glyph cards to suggest transliterations for individual symbols and Gloss cards to propose meanings for entire words, forming the foundational layer of scholarly interpretation.
	•	Establish Hypotheses: Using Proposal cards, players can advance theories about the manuscript's fundamental nature, such as its origin (Provenance) or the language family it belongs to. These hypotheses shape the strategic direction of the game, making certain translations easier to propose and creating distinct analytical frameworks for the group to follow or contest.
	•	Build Consensus: A robust voting mechanic lies at the center of player interaction. Every major proposal is subject to a vote, forcing players to persuade, collaborate, and compete to advance their theories. Successfully championed proposals reward players with Clout, a measure of academic influence and a key resource for taking more powerful actions.
	•	Achieve Victory: Success is not singular. Players can win by achieving the ultimate group goal: successfully verifying a full and correct translation of the manuscript. Alternatively, if the evidence suggests the manuscript is an elaborate hoax, a player can win by exposing the fraud and correctly identifying the perpetrator among the historical figures.
The resulting experience is a unique blend of genres. The gameplay combines the collaborative but secret-driventension of a game like Arkham Horror with the clever bluffing and rules shenanigans found in Sheriff of Nottingham. This fusion of mechanics creates a consistently engaging and unpredictable social environment.
These core mechanics serve as the foundation for a set of standout features that give The Voynich Game its unique and powerful position in the market.
3.0 Key Differentiators: A Game Designed for Enduring Engagement
The following features are not merely clever mechanics; they are the foundational pillars of the game's design, engineered to create a deeply replayable, thematically resonant, and eminently marketable product that stands apart from any other game on the shelf.
Unparalleled Thematic Depth Through Historical Grounding
The Voynich Game immerses players in a rich, historical narrative by moving beyond generic roles. Players embody the actual historical figures whose lives and careers intersected with the manuscript, each bringing the worldview and methodologies of their era to the table. This is not just flavor text; it is mechanically integrated into the core experience.
Key historical personas players can assume include:
	•	Wilfrid Voynich, the antiquarian who brought the manuscript to modern fame.
	•	Athanasius Kircher, the 17th-century Jesuit scholar who famously attempted to decipher it.
	•	Sir Francis Bacon, the Renaissance philosopher and father of the scientific method.
	•	Ethel Lilian Voynich, the novelist and revolutionary with her own ties to the mystery.
This list represents just a fraction of the full roster, which includes dozens of other meticulously researched figures such as the alchemist John Dee, pioneering cryptanalyst Elizebeth Friedman, and revolutionary Nestor Makhno, ensuring a vast and varied cast for players to explore.
Each character possesses unique goals and asymmetric abilities tied directly to their historical context. Wilfrid Voynich’s goal to "Translate & Sell" creates a different strategic approach than the "Ladies of the Order" who seek to "Endure & Be Heard," the WWI-era scholar who must "Translate & Survive," or the modern "Internet Researcher" focused on "Translate & Gain Clout," ensuring that a player's identity fundamentally shapes their path to victory.
Infinite Replayability by Design
The game is built on a modular framework that guarantees no two sessions are ever the same. The Era and Locale rule system allows players to combine different historical periods and settings, creating "significantly different game play" with each unique pairing. A game set in the court of Rudolf II in Prague will feel completely different from one played among modern cryptographers.
Furthermore, we are introducing an innovative production concept: randomized rulebooks in each boxed set. Each copy of the game will ship with a different combination of Era and Locale rules, making each individual box a unique experience out of the gate. This feature promotes organic variety and ensures a vibrant ecosystem of play styles from the moment of release.
Revolutionary "Hidden Content" Mechanics
The game’s most powerful marketing hook is its integration of discoverable "hidden content"—a game within the game. Key cards in every set will be printed with fluorescing ink, revealing an entirely new layer of symbols, clues, and even rules when viewed under a blacklight. This feature is not an afterthought but a core design principle intended to generate excitement and mystique.
Other hidden content concepts include:
	•	"Magic Eye" patterns concealed on the backs of cards.
	•	3D anaglyphs that reveal hidden images when viewed with special glasses.
The strategic value of this approach is immense. This system is "designed with community legend-building and gameplay rumors in mind." The organic discovery of these secrets by players will fuel online discussion, create fan theories, and drive "high curiosity," transforming the player base into a self-sustaining marketing engine.
These unique differentiators are central to our commercial strategy for establishing The Voynich Game as a premier brand in tabletop gaming.
4.0 The Strategic Vision: Building a Community and a Brand
The Voynich Game is conceived not as a single product, but as a platform for building a long-term, profitable brand with a deeply invested community. Its core design elements are strategically aligned to generate sustained interest and create multiple avenues for future growth.
Fostering a Self-Sustaining Player Community
The game's central mystery and revolutionary hidden content mechanics are engineered to produce powerful, organic, word-of-mouth marketing. The thrill of discovering a secret blacklight clue or a hidden "Magic Eye" pattern is a shareable moment that players will be eager to discuss.
This process will naturally fuel online forums, social media groups, and fan-run wikis dedicated to unraveling the game's deepest secrets, mirroring the real-world community dedicated to the manuscript itself. This player-driven engagement creates a powerful and persistent marketing engine at minimal ongoing cost, continuously drawing new players into the game's ecosystem.
A Robust and Scalable Expansion Model
The modular design of The Voynich Game makes it exceptionally expansion-ready. The Era and Locale system provides a clear and logical framework for introducing new content. We envision a steady release schedule of inexpensive expansions that introduce:
	•	New Eras and Locales, altering the game's core rules and feel.
	•	New historical characters with unique goals and abilities.
	•	New language hypotheses and translation card sets.
This model provides a clear, long-tail revenue stream while continuously re-engaging the core player base with fresh content, ensuring the brand remains vital and relevant for years to come.
This strategic vision underpins our belief in the project's exceptional market potential.
5.0 Partnership Opportunity and Next Steps
In summary, The Voynich Game represents a rare opportunity to launch a product with a globally recognized and captivating theme, deeply engaging and replayable mechanics, and an innovative, self-perpetuating marketing engine built directly into its design. It is a game engineered for both critical acclaim and commercial longevity.
We are currently seeking investment or a strategic marketing partnership to bring this unique vision to the global tabletop market. We are confident that with the right partner, The Voynich Game can become a landmark title that captures the imagination of players worldwide.
We invite you to schedule a follow-up discussion to explore this compelling opportunity in greater detail.
4 Surprising Design Choices That Make 'The Voynich Game' a Work of Genius
For centuries, the Voynich Manuscript has been the ultimate intellectual puzzle box—a medieval book filled with unidentifiable plants, strange diagrams, and written in a language no one has ever been able to read. Scholars, cryptographers, and amateurs have dedicated their lives to cracking its code, but it remains one of history's most compelling unsolved mysteries.
This presents a fascinating challenge for a designer. How do you create a game about a puzzle that may have no solution? The answer, it turns out, is to not make a game about the puzzle at all. This post will explore four of the most surprising and brilliant design takeaways from a deep analysis of "The Voynich Game," a complex and intriguing tabletop concept that simulates the mystery rather than trying to solve it.
1. It's Not a Puzzle, It's an Academic Battlefield
The first and most critical design decision was to reject the premise of a solvable puzzle entirely. Instead of a straightforward code-breaking exercise, the game’s core loop brilliantly reframes the objective around consensus-building. Players use Voynichese word cards as raw material, proposing translations with Glyph cards (which represent individual symbols) and Gloss cards (which define entire words). But here’s the twist: players must also establish the manuscript's Provenance—its historical origin—and fight over competing Language Hypotheses. All of these theories are then put to a group vote.
The designer's core challenge was to gamify a puzzle with no known solution. The genius of The Voynich Game is that it shifts the victory condition from "finding the right answer" to "making your answer the accepted one." Success isn't measured by being correct but by persuading your peers, thereby gaining Clout. This Clout resource is a brilliant abstraction of academic capital—a stand-in for prestige, citations, and institutional power. This mechanic cleverly simulates the real-world dynamics of academic research, turning the table into a microcosm of "actual academic disputes and collaborative/competitive dynamics of decipherment."
2. You Play as an Entire Era, Not Just a Character
In The Voynich Game, players don't just take on generic roles; they embody specific historical figures whose worldviews are baked into their actions. These characters—from Francis Bacon and Athanasius Kircher to Wilfrid Voynich himself—aren't just skins for a set of abilities. They represent the entire intellectual and philosophical framework of their time. Even more, characters have dual-sided cards, allowing them to flip between their historical persona and a modern academic alter ego.
An example round illustrates this perfectly. Francis Bacon might use "showmanship" to force a blind vote on a shaky theory. Athanasius Kircher, the 17th-century Jesuit polymath, flips his card to become a Jesuit linguist and proposes a "proto-Hebraic mystical language," weaving together disparate symbols into a grand, persuasive vision. Wilfrid Voynich acts opportunistically, with a "hint of forgery paranoia." And in a stroke of genius, a modern "Internet Conspiracy Theorist" can join the fray, sowing "epistemological chaos" by corrupting data. This approach transforms the game from a simple tactical puzzle into a living simulation of intellectual history, where players must contend not just with each other, but with the very limits and biases of their character's worldview. Each character becomes a reflection of the "epistemic mood of their era."
3. The Game Is Designed to Create Its Own Real-World Mysteries
Perhaps the most meta and brilliant aspect of The Voynich Game is how it mirrors the real manuscript's legacy of rumor and legend. The game is designed with built-in secrets intended to spill out from the box and into the player community. These mechanics include:
	•	Cards with hidden content that can only be revealed by blacklight.
	•	Hidden images or rules based on "Magic Eye" patterns on card backs.
	•	Randomized rulebooks included in different boxed sets, creating organic variety and preventing any single group from having the "complete" version of the game.
These features are intentionally designed to foster "community legend-building and gameplay rumors." Players might hear about a blacklight expansion from a friend or discover a Magic Eye pattern by chance, creating exactly the kind of intrigue that has kept the actual Voynich Manuscript famous for centuries.
Brilliant for a Voynich-themed game.
4. You Might Be a Scholar... or a Fraud
The game adds a powerful layer of social deduction through bluffing and asymmetric goals. Different characters have different victory conditions; Wilfrid Voynich, for instance, has the simple goal to "Translate & Sell," reflecting his commercial interests. But the ultimate twist comes from the Author Card.
At a certain point, one player might secretly draw this card, revealing that they are the original author of the manuscript—a fraud. Their goal instantly shifts. To win, they must conceal their identity by actively voting against correct translations and misleading the group. This mechanic is the game's ultimate commentary on the manuscript itself, forcing the central question of "is it real or a hoax?" directly into the gameplay loop and making one player the living embodiment of that uncertainty. This transforms the game into a system of "collaborative but secret-driven" play, reminiscent of games like Arkham Horror crossed with the bluffing and rule-bending of Sheriff of Nottingham.
Conclusion: A Game About How We Make Meaning
Tying these elements together, The Voynich Game reveals itself to be something far more profound than a game about an old book. It's a deep and insightful simulation of the very human process of creating knowledge. It explores how we build consensus, how personal ambition shapes the search for truth, and how we navigate profound uncertainty. The design brilliantly shifts the focus from the what (the manuscript's meaning) to the how (how we decide what things mean).
The game's design forces us to ask: when we confront the unknown, are we truly uncovering a hidden truth, or are we just building a story that we can all agree on?

The Voynich Game: System Specification Document
1.0 Game Overview & Core Vision
This document details the complete mechanical and systematic framework for The Voynich Game, a tabletop experience centered on the collaborative and competitive decipherment of the world's most mysterious manuscript. The game's design is engineered to marry deep thematic immersion—drawing from the real-world history, figures, and academic debates surrounding the Voynich Manuscript—with a robust strategic gameplay engine. Players will navigate centuries of scholarly intrigue, forming and breaking alliances to either uncover a profound historical truth or expose a masterful fraud.
The high-level specifications of the game are as follows:
	•	Game Concept: To collectively and competitively decipher the Voynich Manuscript by proposing and verifying translations, establishing foundational hypotheses, and voting on the validity of scholarly claims.
	•	Player Dynamics: A unique blend of collaborative research, where players build upon each other's work, and competitive, secret-driven goals, where individual ambitions and hidden roles can shift the course of history.
	•	Core Engine: A card-based system driven by linguistic logic, the strategic preservation and transfer of information across historical eras, and a central social deduction mechanic based on achieving scholarly consensus.
	•	Winning the Game: Victory is achieved by reaching one of two end-states: either a player or group achieves a verified full translation of the manuscript through the Consensus & Voting system, or a player successfully identifies the perpetrator of a fraud, as determined by the secret Author Card mechanic.
These specifications are built upon a set of foundational concepts that serve as the pillars of the gameplay experience.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2.0 Foundational Game Concepts
This section breaks down the key conceptual pillars that define the strategic landscape of The Voynich Game. A firm grasp of these concepts is crucial for understanding the intricate interplay between players, their resources, and their interaction with the game's central, enigmatic puzzle.
The Manuscript Pool The Manuscript Pool is the shared central play area where all untranslated Voynichese Word Cards are played. This pool represents the collective body of knowledge about the manuscript itself, forming the evolving puzzle that all players are working to solve. Actions taken by players will primarily target or build upon the cards within this pool.
Clout & Backing These are the two primary resources players manage. Clout is a measure of academic prestige, reputation, and influence within the scholarly community; it is often gained through successful proposals or specific card effects. Backing represents institutional support, funding, and the general capacity to perform work. It is spent in the form of chits, with each chit typically funding one standard action. The more Backing a player has, the more they can accomplish on their turn.
Consensus & Voting This is the central social mechanic of the game. When a player proposes a significant translation or a major hypothesis, a vote is triggered among the players. Achieving "Consensus" is a powerful event; it can grant the proposing player rewards and makes all future actions related to that hypothesis significantly easier, often converting them into free actions for all players. This system simulates the process of peer review and the formation of academic paradigms.
Provenance & Hypotheses These represent the two main theories that players work to establish. Provenance is a hypothesis about the origin, or source, of the manuscript. Language Hypotheses are theories about the specific language the manuscript is written in or the cipher used to encode it. Establishing consensus on these foundational theories is a critical step toward a successful translation.
Eras & Chronological Play The game is structured chronologically. Each player embodies a character from a specific historical period, and players are seated in order from the earliest era to the latest. This seating order affects the flow of information; players in the "past" (to the left) can use Preservation cards to save clues and translations for players in the "future" (to the right) to discover, simulating the passage of knowledge through time.
Dual Player Roles (Character & Academic) Each player card is two-sided, representing a dual role. The Characterside represents a specific historical persona with unique goals and abilities. The Academic side represents their modern scholarly counterpart. This system is designed to create a core strategic tension; players must choose whether to engage with the manuscript's historical context directly (as the Character) or to engage with the meta-puzzle of academic theory and peer review (as the Academic). Flipping their card during a turn is a strategic choice to access different sets of actions, reflecting the distinction between direct historical action and modern scholarly analysis.
These core concepts are brought to life through the game's primary components: the card ecosystem.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3.0 Game Components: The Card Ecosystem
The cards are the primary engine of The Voynich Game, driving every action from proposing a simple transliteration to altering the fundamental rules of play. This section provides a comprehensive catalog of all card types, analyzing how each one contributes to the game's mechanical depth and thematic narrative.
Card Type	Core Function	Example(s)
Word Card	The central puzzle pieces. Untranslated Voynichese words that are played into the Manuscript Pool to be decoded.	fchorchdy
Glyph Chit	Proposes a transliteration for a single Voynichese symbol. The foundational layer of translation.	“𐑒 = K”
Gloss Card	Proposes a full word translation, building upon Glyph transliterations. The primary tool for solving the puzzle.	“fchorchdy = ‘sacred salve’”; "Old High German: WERALT : WORLD"
Proposal Card	Puts forth a major theory about the manuscript's origin (Provenance) or language. Used to establish a consensus.	“Proposal: Language = Old High German”
Preservation Card	Allows a player to store (cache) other cards (like Gloss or Clue cards) for later use or for future players to find. Introduces strategic planning and information hiding.	Amphora, Tome
Evidence Card	Supports or refutes a hypothesis or translation, adding weight to votes and building a case for a specific theory.	“Alder Pollen”, “Pollen Match: Strong match with 15th century Bohemian flora”
Investigation Card	Grants special actions related to discovery, such as searching discard piles or gaining clout from a specific field of study.	Cryptography, Unknown Botanical Sample, Palynology
Contact Card	Allows a player to gain clues or access knowledge from fields of study outside their character's expertise, adding strategic flexibility.	“Contact: Forensic Botanist”
Character Card	Defines the player's asymmetric historical persona, including their unique goals, abilities, and era.	Wilfrid Voynich, Athanasius Kircher
Author Card	A secret role card. If drawn, that player is secretly the manuscript's author, introducing a hidden traitor/bluffing mechanic with specific voting restrictions.	Author Card Wilfrid Voynich
Backing Card	Grants resources, typically Clout chits or extra actions, representing institutional support or academic funding.	“Grant: The British Museum will fund 2 extra actions...”
Voting Rules Card	A card that temporarily or permanently alters the rules for how consensus votes are conducted.	“Rule Change”
Page Card	Thematic cards that provide a free action if their subject (e.g., Herbal, Cosmological) is the dominant evidence type in the Manuscript Pool.	Pharmaceutical, Herbal, Cosmological
Fragment Card	A minor thematic component, often played for a free, small effect that contributes to the overall puzzle.	Manuscript Fragment
Era/Locale Rule Card	Defines specific rules, tools, and worldviews for a given historical period or setting in Milieu-style games.	“Renaissance – Alchemy permitted as valid evidence...”
The following section will detail how these components are arranged to begin a game.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4.0 Game Setup & Structure
The setup phase is critical, as it establishes the game's style, assigns player roles, and constructs the chronological framework that will govern the flow of play and information throughout the session.
	1.	Choose Game Style: Before the game begins, players must select one of two styles. The decision is typically made by the player holding a Voynich Scholar Card with the most marks; otherwise, it is determined by an opening hand or consensus.
	•	Cross-Era Game: This is the standard style, played according to the base rulebook, featuring characters from disparate historical periods interacting across time.
	•	Milieu Game: This style uses a specific Era Rule Book and Locale Rule Book to create a more focused and thematic setting, with unique rules and mechanics tailored to that specific time and place.
	2.	Assign Characters: Each player chooses or is randomly assigned a Character Card. This card dictates their historical persona, special abilities, and potential victory conditions for the game.
	3.	Establish Seating Order: Players arrange themselves at the table chronologically, from left to right, according to their character's historical era (e.g., a 15th-century character sits to the left of a 17th-century character). For gameplay purposes, players to one's left are considered to be in the "past," while players to one's right are in the "future."
	4.	Prepare Decks and Pools: The central Manuscript common pool area is cleared, and the main deck of cards is shuffled. Players are dealt their starting hands according to the rules of the chosen game style.
With the historical stage set, the game begins its dynamic progression through the ages.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5.0 Gameplay Flow: A Round in Detail
A round in The Voynich Game is a chronological progression of turns, moving from the earliest era player to the latest. Each player takes actions that can have cascading effects, as a discovery or theory proposed in one era can influence the options and information available to players in subsequent eras. For example, Sir Francis Bacon (early 1600s) might propose a theory that Athanasius Kircher (mid-1600s) can then build upon, while Wilfrid Voynich (early 1900s) may "preserve" a key clue that a 21st-century theorist can later unearth.
An individual player's turn is structured into the following phases:
	1.	Expand the Pool This is a mandatory free action. If the card drawn during the "Draw one card" free action is a Voynichese Word Card, it must be played immediately into the Manuscript Pool, expanding the collective puzzle for everyone.
	2.	Take Actions A player may take a number of actions based on their available resources, primarily Backing chits. Actions are divided into two types:
	•	Free Actions: These do not cost Backing and can be performed as specified.
	•	Draw one card from the deck.
	•	Play any card that has been designated as a free action (e.g., through a previously established consensus).
	•	Play one card from their personal cache if enabled by a Preservation card's effect.
	•	Standard Actions (Cost: 1 Backing Chit): These are the core strategic moves a player can make by spending one Backing chit per action.
	•	Propose a full word translation by playing a Gloss Card.
	•	Propose a single-symbol transliteration by playing a Glyph Chit.
	•	Play a Rule Change card to alter the voting mechanics.
	•	Flip their Character/Academic Card to switch roles and access different abilities.
	•	Preserve a clue by playing a card from their hand into their personal cache under a Preservation card.
	3.	Upkeep In the final phase of a turn, players perform any necessary cleanup. This may include flipping their Character/Academic card back to its default side as per card instructions or other end-of-turn effects.
This turn structure provides the framework for the game's most critical and interactive mechanical systems.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6.0 Core Mechanics Deep Dive
Mastery of The Voynich Game requires a deep understanding of its pivotal systems. This section provides a detailed codification of the game's most crucial mechanics, outlining their rules and strategic implications.
The Translation Process Translation is a two-layered process that forms the game's central puzzle.
	1.	First, players propose transliterations for individual Voynichese symbols by playing Glyph Chits onto Word Cardsin the Manuscript Pool. This establishes a foundational "alphabet" for a given word.
	2.	Next, players can propose a full word translation by playing a Gloss Card. For a Gloss Card to be successful, it should align with previously accepted Glyph Chits. As a strategic incentive for collaboration, whenever a Gloss Card is successfully played using another player's glyph, the originator of that Glyph Chit is rewarded with Backing chits.
The Consensus & Voting System Voting is triggered whenever a player proposes a major translation or a foundational hypothesis (such as the manuscript's language or provenance). The outcome of the vote has significant consequences:
	•	Consensus Achieved: If the proposal gains consensus (e.g., via majority vote), the proposer may be rewarded with an extra turn. More importantly, actions related to the newly accepted hypothesis (such as playing Gloss Cards in the consensus language) become easier, often becoming free actions for all players.
	•	Consensus Fails: If the proposal is voted down, the proposer faces a penalty, such as losing their next turn. This mechanic forces players to carefully consider when to put forth a theory and to lobby for support from their peers.
Preservation & Information Transfer This mechanic allows for the strategic management and transfer of information across time. Using Preservation Cards like an Amphora or Tome, a player can create a personal Cache in front of them.
	•	Placing Cards: A player can spend an action to place cards (such as valuable Gloss or Clue cards) from their hand into their Cache.
	•	Sealing: Some Preservation cards can be "Sealed," protecting the information within but preventing further additions.
	•	Retrieval: A player in a "future" era can use Clue Cards to retrieve information from a "past" player's preserved cache, simulating the rediscovery of lost knowledge and creating opportunities for long-term strategic planning.
The Author Mechanic This is a secret role mechanic that introduces an element of bluffing and hidden identity.
	•	Discovery: A player discovers they are the Author by drawing their own character's Author Card during a specific game event (e.g., when calling a vote). Upon doing so, they must secretly search the deck and remove all other Author Cards from the game.
	•	The Critical Choice: The Author must immediately make a binding choice: they will either consistently vote against any theory that points to their true identity (concealing it), or they will consistently vote for such theories (revealing it). They cannot alternate between these strategies.
	•	Final Round: The Author secretly sets aside a special hand of seven cards, which replaces their normal hand during the game's Final Round, giving them a powerful, hidden advantage in the endgame.
These mechanics find their most unique expression through the game's diverse and asymmetric cast of characters.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7.0 The Characters of the Game
The asymmetric characters are central to the experience of The Voynich Game. Each historical figure provides a unique lens through which to play, complete with distinct thematic contexts, special abilities, and personalized victory conditions that shape their strategic approach to deciphering the manuscript.

All character information is presented to players in a streamlined, two-sided format designed to be clear and concise for at-a-glance reference during play.

	•	Acquisition Instinct: You may draw 2 cards when you search a discard or archive pile; keep one.
	•	Provenance Play: Once per game, you may reassign authorship of a card in the Manuscript Pool. Gain +1 Clout if your claim is not challenged.
	•	Passive
	•	Bookseller’s Cache: You may preserve up to 3 cards (instead of 2). Preserved cards may include Proposals or Clue cards.

	•	Win if you end the game with the Voynich Manuscript in hand and 3 or more preserved cards attributed to different eras.
This character-driven system is designed for long-term engagement, supported by a plan for future content and hidden discoveries.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
8.0 Expansions and Hidden Content
The Voynich Game is designed as a living product, built for long-term discovery, replayability, and community engagement. The base game itself contains secrets waiting to be unlocked, and its modular design ensures a framework for future growth and new mysteries.
Front-Loaded Expansions
A core feature of the game is the inclusion of hidden content within the starter set, intended to be discovered by players through gameplay or chance. This creates a sense of genuine mystery and rewards dedicated investigation.
	•	Blacklight Content: Select cards are overprinted with fluorescing ink that is invisible under normal light. When viewed with a black light, this ink reveals an entirely new layer of the game—new symbols, clues, or rules. To fully utilize this content, players will need a special rule book, The Blacklight Rule Tome.
	•	3D Anaglyphs: Some cards will contain hidden images or text that can only be seen when viewed with special anaglyph (red/cyan) glasses.
	•	"Magic Eye" Content: Autostereograms, or "Magic Eye" patterns, will be concealed within the designs on the backs of the cards, hiding secret patterns, rules, or clues for observant players.
Future Expansions
The game's modular design allows for a robust schedule of future content to keep the experience fresh and engaging. A key design feature is that the distribution of rulebooks within each boxed set will be randomized, creating an organic variety across copies of the game and fostering a unique sense of community discovery. Planned expansions include:
	•	Inexpensive Era and Locale rule sets that can be mixed and matched to create new Milieu Game settings.
	•	Major expansions featuring entirely new languages, new historical and fictional characters, and new settingsthat introduce novel mechanics and challenges.
This commitment to evolving content ensures that the central theme of the game—the thrill of discovery in the face of an endless mystery—remains at the heart of every session.
A Round in The Voynich Game: A Walkthrough for New Players
1.0 Introduction: Setting the Scene
Welcome, aspiring scholars and decipherers, to the enigmatic world of The Voynich Game. This guide is designed to walk you through a complete round of play, demonstrating the core mechanics, strategic depth, and unique character interactions that make each session a new puzzle. Our goal is to illuminate the flow of the game, from a player's first action to the state of the board at the round's end.
For this walkthrough, we will follow four players who have taken on the roles of historical figures connected to the manuscript's long and mysterious history. They are seated in chronological order, a key rule that influences how information can be passed from the past to the future.
Here are our players for the round:
Player Seat	Character	Primary Goal
Player 1	John Dee (1527–1609)	Pursue esoteric wisdom
Player 2	Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680)	Win when confusion triumphs over clarity
Player 3	Wilfrid Voynich (1865–1930)	Translate & Sell
Player 4	Internet Conspiracy Theorist (21st Century)	Translate & Gain Clout
With our cast of characters established, let's examine the state of the game as the first round begins.
2.0 The State of Play: The Round Begins
The table is set, the cards are dealt, and the central mystery—the manuscript itself—lies open for interpretation. At the start of this round, the situation is as follows:
	•	Manuscript Pool: Three untranslated Voynichese Word cards are face-up in the center of the table. These are the core puzzle pieces our players will attempt to solve.
	•	Consensus: No language or provenance hypotheses have been proposed yet, let alone reached consensus. The field is wide open, and any theory is as plausible as the next.
	•	Player Hands: Each player holds a hand of cards containing a mix of Glyph cards (for transliterating single characters), Gloss cards (for translating whole words), and other unique cards that will aid their strategies.
The first move belongs to the player from the earliest era. All eyes now turn to the Elizabethan mystic, John Dee.
3.0 Player 1: John Dee (16th Century) - The Mystic Scholar's Opening
	1.	Objective & Strategy: John Dee's primary goal is the "pursuit of esoteric wisdom." His strategy is not necessarily to find the most logical translation, but one that aligns with his mystical and alchemical worldview. He will aim to anchor the group's interpretation in this esoteric framework from the very beginning.
	2.	Turn Actions:
	1.	Draws a Card: As his free action, Dee draws a card, adding it to his hand.
	2.	Proposes a Transliteration: He spends his first standard action to play a Glyph Card onto one of the Voynichese Word cards in the pool. This is the first, foundational step of translation—proposing that a single, unknown Voynichese character corresponds to a known letter.
	3.	Makes a Mystical Connection: Dee immediately follows up with his second standard action. He selects a Gloss Card from his hand that proposes a full translation for that same word, building on the glyph he just established. He explains his reasoning to the table:
	4.	End of Turn: Having laid the first stones on the path of an alchemical interpretation, Dee ends his turn.
	3.	Turn Summary: Dee's turn was a classic opening move. He did not propose a full language or force a vote on a grand theory. Instead, he successfully established a partial translation, anchoring one of the key puzzle words to his mystical perspective. He hopes this initial interpretation will influence all future attempts to translate related words.
With the first theory on the table, play passes to the next scholar in the timeline: the Jesuit polymath, Athanasius Kircher.
4.0 Player 2: Athanasius Kircher (17th Century) - The Master of Obscure Knowledge
	1.	Objective & Strategy: Kircher's victory comes not from clarity, but from confusion. His goal is to weave intricate, compelling, but ultimately obfuscating theories. His strategy is to leverage his unique character abilities to make bold claims that bypass the normal, evidence-based process.
	2.	Turn Actions:
	1.	Draws a Card: He performs his free draw and adds a Proposal Card to his hand, a perfect tool for his grand plans.
	2.	Invokes a Special Ability: Instead of building on Dee's work, Kircher decides to introduce a competing paradigm. He invokes his character's special ability, Grapholalia. This powerful skill allows him to propose a Gloss or Proposal even without any supporting Glyph cards on the board.
	3.	Proposes a Language: He plays his Proposal Card to formally suggest that the manuscript's language is a "proto-Hebraic mystical language." According to the rules, this grand claim immediately triggers a Scholarly Consensus Vote.
	4.	The Vote: The other players must now vote on Kircher's hypothesis. Dee, invested in his alchemical theory, votes against it. Voynich, ever the pragmatist, sees no commercial advantage in this obscure theory and also votes no. The vote fails to reach consensus.
	5.	Gains Clout from Failure: Here, Kircher's brilliance shines. The text on his Grapholalia ability states that even if his proposal is voted down, he gains +1 Clout for his "compelling confidence." This demonstrates how a character's unique skills can create advantages from seemingly failed actions.
	3.	Turn Summary: Kircher's turn was a masterclass in advancing a personal agenda. While his language proposal failed, he still gained personal influence (Clout), introduced a competing and confusing theory into the debate, and successfully undermined the simple narrative Dee was trying to build. This directly serves his unique victory condition, as described in the source: "Kircher wins when confusion triumphs over clarity." He doesn't need his theory to pass; he just needs to prevent a simple, clear consensus from forming.
Play now moves forward three centuries, to the man who gave the manuscript its name: Wilfrid Voynich.
5.0 Player 3: Wilfrid Voynich (20th Century) - The Cunning Antiquarian
	1.	Objective & Strategy: Wilfrid Voynich is driven by a clear motive: "Translate & Sell." His strategy is less about immediate glory and more about controlling the flow of information. He seeks to acquire valuable knowledge and hide it until its release can bring him the greatest personal gain.
	2.	Turn Actions:
	1.	Draws a Card: Voynich draws a Gloss Card. He immediately recognizes its value—it's a very plausible translation linking a Voynichese word to Old High German, a popular real-world theory.
	2.	Preserves Information: Rather than playing this powerful card and sharing the knowledge, he executes a shrewder move. He spends one action to play a Preservation Card—a Tome—into his personal Cache area. He then spends a second action to place the valuable Old High German Gloss Card face down underneath the Tome.
	3.	The Strategic Insight: This is a pivotal, non-obvious play. By preserving the card, Voynich has effectively removed a key piece of the puzzle from the game. He can reveal it at a dramatic moment to secure a critical vote, gain a massive amount of Clout, or even pass it to a future player as part of a deal. This perfectly reflects his "Translate & Sell" motivation—he is holding onto his "product" until the market is just right.
	3.	Turn Summary: Voynich's turn was quiet but potent. He made no changes to the shared Manuscript Pool, but he has secured a powerful future advantage. His actions demonstrate a completely different path to victory: not through open debate, but through patience, foresight, and the careful hoarding of information.
The round concludes with our final player, a disruptive force from the modern era.
6.0 Player 4: Internet Conspiracy Theorist (21st Century) - The Agent of Chaos
	1.	Objective & Strategy: The Internet Theorist's goal is to "Translate & Gain Clout," but their methods are anything but conventional. Their special ability is to "Corrupt Data," reflecting a strategy of disruption, skepticism, and tearing down established narratives.
	2.	Turn Actions:
	1.	Draws a Card: The player draws an Investigation Card, which might help them uncover hidden facts later.
	2.	Challenges the Narrative: Surveying the board—Dee's nascent mystical theory and Kircher's failed but influential proposal—the player decides to inject chaos. They play a card that allows them to use their special ability: "insert corrupted data."
	3.	The Disruptive Effect: This action directly targets an opponent's work. It forces the Glyph Card that John Dee played to be re-evaluated, triggering a special 'Scholarly Consensus Vote' where players must vote as their academic counterparts to refute it. Seeing the weakness in Dee's unsubstantiated alchemical claim, the other players vote to refute it. The vote succeeds, and Dee's Glyph Card is discarded from the Voynichese Word.
	4.	The Strategic Insight: This action did not advance the Theorist's own translation. Instead, it was a purely negative play designed to undermine an opponent. By removing the foundational glyph, they have also invalidated Dee's Gloss card that was built upon it. This shows how some characters excel at hindering others to gain a relative advantage.
	3.	Turn Summary: The Theorist's turn has reset a portion of the puzzle. They successfully nullified Dee's progress and left the board in a greater state of uncertainty. This chaos directly benefits players like Kircher and creates new openings for players like Voynich to exploit with his hidden knowledge.
The final player's turn is over, bringing the first round of the game to a close.
7.0 End of the Round: A Summary and Key Lessons
The round ends with the manuscript more mysterious than when it began. One scholar's attempt at translation was proposed and then systematically dismantled. A grand linguistic theory failed to gain consensus but paradoxically increased its creator's influence. Meanwhile, a crucial piece of evidence that could clarify the entire puzzle now lies hidden, waiting for the opportune moment to be revealed.
For new players, this round demonstrates several core principles of The Voynich Game:
	•	Characters Drive Asymmetric Strategies: Each player's actions were driven by their character's unique mechanics and goals. Dee's mysticism was expressed by proposing a niche translation. Kircher's obscurantism was enabled by his Grapholalia ability to bypass evidence. Voynich's commercialism was enacted through the Preservation mechanic, and the Theorist's modern skepticism was represented by a 'Corrupt Data' ability that attacked an existing theory.
	•	There Are Many Paths to Influence: Gaining an edge isn't always about winning votes. Kircher gained Cloutfrom a failed proposal by using a special ability. Voynich invested an entire turn not on the board, but on securing a future advantage in his Cache. Success is measured in more than just translated words.
	•	Translation is a Puzzle and a Debate: The core of the game is a two-part process. First, you must propose solutions to the puzzle by playing Glyph and Gloss cards. Second, you must engage in a debate to persuade others of your theories through the game's voting and consensus mechanics.
	•	Information is a Resource: As Wilfrid Voynich's turn perfectly illustrated, knowledge is power. Deciding when to share information or hide it is a key strategic decision. Voynich's move to hide information with a Preservationcard is powerful, but other players can counter it. The source rules mention Investigation and Clue cards that allow players to 'unlock any past player's preserved cards.' Your hidden knowledge is never perfectly safe.
The Voynich Game: A Player's Guide to Card Types
Welcome to the enigmatic world of The Voynich Game. Deciphering one of history's most mysterious manuscripts is a complex task involving linguistic analysis, scholarly debate, and strategic planning. This guide is designed to help new players quickly understand the purpose of each major card type, making your first playthrough smoother and more intuitive by revealing how each piece of the puzzle fits into the grander scheme of discovery.
1. The Core of the Manuscript: Decipherment Cards
These are the fundamental cards you will use in the core gameplay loop. They represent the raw materials of translation—the untranslated words, the proposed sounds of individual symbols, and the suggested meanings of entire words. These cards form the engine of the game's core action economy, costing Standard Actions to place and generating "Backing chits" as rewards. Mastering their interplay is the first step toward cracking the code.
Card Type	Primary Purpose	Illustrative Example
Word Cards	Represent the untranslated words that form the central puzzle.	Use Glyph Chits to Translate
Glyph Cards	Propose a transliteration for a single Voynichese symbol.	"Proposes that a specific glyph should be read as 'K'."
Gloss Cards	Propose a full translation for an entire Voynichese word.	Old High German: WERALT : WORLD
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Word Cards
	•	Purpose: These cards represent the untranslated words from the Voynich manuscript and form the central puzzle that all players work to solve.
	•	Function:
	•	Cost: Mandatory Free Action. While the card template lists "Standard Action," the core rules specify these must be played into the "Manuscript common pool" immediately upon being drawn, which overrides the template cost.
	•	They are the foundational "puzzle pieces" of the game.
	•	Example:
Strategic Tip: A fresh Word card can be a distraction. If other players are close to solving a key word, playing a new, complex one can draw attention away, buying you time to formulate your own translation for the more valuable target.
Glyph Cards
	•	Purpose: These cards are used to propose a transliteration (a corresponding letter or sound) for a single symbol within a Voynichese Word card.
	•	Function:
	•	Cost: 1 Standard Action.
	•	Players play these directly onto a Voynichese Word Card in the common pool.
	•	When a Gloss card matching this Glyph's proposal is played on the same word, the player who played the Glyph card gains a "Backing chit."
	•	A player acting as an "Academic" can refute the proposal, which triggers a Scholarly Consensus Vote.
	•	Example:
Strategic Tip: Use Glyph cards to signal your linguistic intentions or to test the waters. Playing a glyph common in a specific language family can encourage others to follow your lead, or it can be used to bait an opponent into revealing their own theories through a refutation.
Gloss Cards
	•	Purpose: These cards represent a proposed full translation for an entire Voynichese word, often tied to a specific language hypothesis.
	•	Function:
	•	Cost: 1 Standard Action.
	•	They are played on Voynichese Word cards to propose a specific meaning.
	•	Example:
Strategic Tip: Pay attention to the language of the Gloss cards other players are using. A cluster of "Old High German" translations is a strong signal that someone might be preparing to play a Proposal card for that language, which could change the game's entire dynamic.
Laying down multiple Gloss Cards of the same language is the primary way to build momentum for a formal theory. Once the table sees a pattern, you can use a Proposal Card to make that theory official.
2. Building Your Theory: Hypothesis & Evidence Cards
Deciphering words is only part of the puzzle. These cards allow players to build, support, and challenge the larger theories about the manuscript's origin (provenance) and the language in which it is written.
Card Type	Primary Purpose	Illustrative Example

Proposal Cards
	•	Purpose: These cards are used to formally propose a hypothesis about the manuscript's language or provenance (origin).

	•	Purpose: These cards are used to support or challenge existing hypotheses and translations, adding scientific or historical weight to votes and claims.

	•	Purpose: These cards provide a bonus action when a specific type of evidence becomes dominant in the Manuscript Pool, representing a breakthrough in a particular field.

Marketing Proposal: The Voynich Game
1.0 Introduction: The Unsolved Mystery as a Market Opportunity
For centuries, the Voynich Manuscript has remained one of history's most compelling and unyielding enigmas—a book written in an unknown script by an unknown author, filled with illustrations of unidentifiable plants and cryptic diagrams. This real-world mystery is more than a historical curiosity; it is a powerful, untapped narrative engine, perfectly suited for an immersive tabletop experience that challenges players to do what centuries of scholars could not: unravel its secrets.
This proposal introduces The Voynich Game, a strategically deep and thematically rich game designed to capture the academic rivalries, collaborative breakthroughs, and deceptive dead-ends of the global effort to decipher the manuscript. Our objective is to outline the game's unique design, its significant potential for commercial success, and its inherent capacity for fostering passionate community engagement.
We will now detail how The Voynich Game translates this historical intrigue into a compelling and unforgettable core gameplay experience.
2.0 The Core Experience: Decipher, Deceive, and Discover
The strategic heart of The Voynich Game is its core gameplay loop, a system meticulously designed to simulate the real-world dynamics of academic research. It is an environment of intense competition and fragile alliances, where players must navigate scholarly disputes, forge consensus, and guard against misinformation in a shared quest for the truth. This loop transforms the solitary act of deciphering a text into a dynamic social and strategic challenge.
The game's central actions are designed to be intuitive yet layered, creating a cycle of proposal, debate, and discovery:
	•	Confront the Manuscript: Players begin by drawing and playing Voynichese Word cards into a shared pool, creating the central, unsolved text that the group must collectively decipher.
	•	Propose Meanings: Players use Glyph cards to suggest transliterations for individual symbols and Gloss cards to propose meanings for entire words, forming the foundational layer of scholarly interpretation.
	•	Establish Hypotheses: Using Proposal cards, players can advance theories about the manuscript's fundamental nature, such as its origin (Provenance) or the language family it belongs to. These hypotheses shape the strategic direction of the game, making certain translations easier to propose and creating distinct analytical frameworks for the group to follow or contest.
	•	Build Consensus: A robust voting mechanic lies at the center of player interaction. Every major proposal is subject to a vote, forcing players to persuade, collaborate, and compete to advance their theories. Successfully championed proposals reward players with Clout, a measure of academic influence and a key resource for taking more powerful actions.
	•	Achieve Victory: Success is not singular. Players can win by achieving the ultimate group goal: successfully verifying a full and correct translation of the manuscript. Alternatively, if the evidence suggests the manuscript is an elaborate hoax, a player can win by exposing the fraud and correctly identifying the perpetrator among the historical figures.
The resulting experience is a unique blend of genres. The gameplay combines the collaborative but secret-driventension of a game like Arkham Horror with the clever bluffing and rules shenanigans found in Sheriff of Nottingham. This fusion of mechanics creates a consistently engaging and unpredictable social environment.
These core mechanics serve as the foundation for a set of standout features that give The Voynich Game its unique and powerful position in the market.
3.0 Key Differentiators: A Game Designed for Enduring Engagement
The following features are not merely clever mechanics; they are the foundational pillars of the game's design, engineered to create a deeply replayable, thematically resonant, and eminently marketable product that stands apart from any other game on the shelf.
Unparalleled Thematic Depth Through Historical Grounding
The Voynich Game immerses players in a rich, historical narrative by moving beyond generic roles. Players embody the actual historical figures whose lives and careers intersected with the manuscript, each bringing the worldview and methodologies of their era to the table. This is not just flavor text; it is mechanically integrated into the core experience.
Key historical personas players can assume include:
	•	Wilfrid Voynich, the antiquarian who brought the manuscript to modern fame.
	•	Athanasius Kircher, the 17th-century Jesuit scholar who famously attempted to decipher it.

Each character possesses unique goals and asymmetric abilities tied directly to their historical context. These unique differentiators are central to our commercial strategy for establishing The Voynich Game as a premier brand in tabletop gaming.

4 Surprising Design Choices That Make 'The Voynich Game' a Work of Genius
For centuries, the Voynich Manuscript has been the ultimate intellectual puzzle box—a medieval book filled with unidentifiable plants, strange diagrams, and written in a language no one has ever been able to read. Scholars, cryptographers, and amateurs have dedicated their lives to cracking its code, but it remains one of history's most compelling unsolved mysteries.
This presents a fascinating challenge for a designer. How do you create a game about a puzzle that may have no solution? The answer, it turns out, is to not make a game about the puzzle at all. This post will explore four of the most surprising and brilliant design takeaways from a deep analysis of "The Voynich Game," a complex and intriguing tabletop concept that simulates the mystery rather than trying to solve it.
1. It's Not a Puzzle, It's an Academic Battlefield
The first and most critical design decision was to reject the premise of a solvable puzzle entirely. Instead of a straightforward code-breaking exercise, the game’s core loop brilliantly reframes the objective around consensus-building. Players use Voynichese word cards as raw material, proposing translations with Glyph cards (which represent individual symbols) and Gloss cards (which define entire words). But here’s the twist: players must also establish the manuscript's Provenance—its historical origin—and fight over competing Language Hypotheses. All of these theories are then put to a group vote.
The designer's core challenge was to gamify a puzzle with no known solution. The genius of The Voynich Game is that it shifts the victory condition from "finding the right answer" to "making your answer the accepted one." Success isn't measured by being correct but by persuading your peers, thereby gaining Clout. This Clout resource is a brilliant abstraction of academic capital—a stand-in for prestige, citations, and institutional power. This mechanic cleverly simulates the real-world dynamics of academic research, turning the table into a microcosm of "actual academic disputes and collaborative/competitive dynamics of decipherment."
2. You Play as an Entire Era, Not Just a Character
In The Voynich Game, players don't just take on generic roles; they embody specific historical figures whose worldviews are baked into their actions. These characters—from Francis Bacon and Athanasius Kircher to Wilfrid Voynich himself—aren't just skins for a set of abilities. They represent the entire intellectual and philosophical framework of their time. Even more, characters have dual-sided cards, allowing them to flip between their historical persona and a modern academic alter ego.
An example round illustrates this perfectly. Francis Bacon might use "showmanship" to force a blind vote on a shaky theory. Athanasius Kircher, the 17th-century Jesuit polymath, flips his card to become a Jesuit linguist and proposes a "proto-Hebraic mystical language," weaving together disparate symbols into a grand, persuasive vision. Wilfrid Voynich acts opportunistically, with a "hint of forgery paranoia." And in a stroke of genius, a modern "Internet Conspiracy Theorist" can join the fray, sowing "epistemological chaos" by corrupting data. This approach transforms the game from a simple tactical puzzle into a living simulation of intellectual history, where players must contend not just with each other, but with the very limits and biases of their character's worldview. Each character becomes a reflection of the "epistemic mood of their era."
3. The Game Is Designed to Create Its Own Real-World Mysteries
Perhaps the most meta and brilliant aspect of The Voynich Game is how it mirrors the real manuscript's legacy of rumor and legend. The game is designed with built-in secrets intended to spill out from the box and into the player community. These mechanics include:
	•	Cards with hidden content that can only be revealed by blacklight.
	•	Hidden images or rules based on "Magic Eye" patterns on card backs.
	•	Randomized rulebooks included in different boxed sets, creating organic variety and preventing any single group from having the "complete" version of the game.
These features are intentionally designed to foster "community legend-building and gameplay rumors." Players might hear about a blacklight expansion from a friend or discover a Magic Eye pattern by chance, creating exactly the kind of intrigue that has kept the actual Voynich Manuscript famous for centuries.
Brilliant for a Voynich-themed game.
4. You Might Be a Scholar... or a Fraud
The game adds a powerful layer of social deduction through bluffing and asymmetric goals. Different characters have different victory conditions; Wilfrid Voynich, for instance, has the simple goal to "Translate & Sell," reflecting his commercial interests. But the ultimate twist comes from the Author Card.
At a certain point, one player might secretly draw this card, revealing that they are the original author of the manuscript—a fraud. Their goal instantly shifts. To win, they must conceal their identity by actively voting against correct translations and misleading the group. This mechanic is the game's ultimate commentary on the manuscript itself, forcing the central question of "is it real or a hoax?" directly into the gameplay loop and making one player the living embodiment of that uncertainty. This transforms the game into a system of "collaborative but secret-driven" play, reminiscent of games like Arkham Horror crossed with the bluffing and rule-bending of Sheriff of Nottingham.
Conclusion: A Game About How We Make Meaning
Tying these elements together, The Voynich Game reveals itself to be something far more profound than a game about an old book. It's a deep and insightful simulation of the very human process of creating knowledge. It explores how we build consensus, how personal ambition shapes the search for truth, and how we navigate profound uncertainty. The design brilliantly shifts the focus from the what (the manuscript's meaning) to the how (how we decide what things mean).
The game's design forces us to ask: when we confront the unknown, are we truly uncovering a hidden truth, or are we just building a story that we can all agree on?

VOYNICH GAME

The base game should be fairly light weight and accessible, but the more you play, the more mysteries are revealed, which adds layers to gameplay, and build into a much heavier weight game, or at least, the option to play it as a more heavyweight game. 

TRANSLATION 
As various translation proposals for words build up, the Maniscript Pool will evolve into what could be a sensible phrase, or could be nonsense. In order to be a successful translation, a manuscript language proposal must 1) match a majority (but need not match all) of the proposed glosses 2) must be built of the glosses proposed by being played on the manuscript pool words, and 3) must successfully win a consensus vote according to the voting rules in play. 

THE WIN DECK
If the players successfully translate the manuscript, they get to play a win round. There is a special deck just for this round, which operates as a reveal about the true nature of the manuscript. The core set comes with “The Order’s Secret Waterworks” win deck. The final round is only played with one or two cards per player, thus the reveal is surprising and mysterious with each game play, and depending upon how the win deck cards interact, there may be variable solutions to the mystery. However, many other win decks could be purchased as expansions with very different win game scenarios. 
Maybe—End Game scenarios are one of two things: Either somebody proves the manuscript is a hoax or gibberish, in which case they win and that’s the end of the game, or players arrive at a successful translation, revealing the existence of the win deck (maybe the win deck is hidden in the packaging with a win deck rulebook and not advertised, so it’s a really surprising reveal. The clues must be pieced together to come to the conclusion that the win deck even exists. The win deck rulebook should strongly request that players keep its existence secret. Perhaps some of the cards in the win deck could have codes which provide a discount on expansion packs?

3	STANDARD ACTIONS [1 Backing chit unless otherwise specified]
	 - Propose a partial translation by playing a Gloss Card. If playing as your Character, play Gloss Card face-down on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Character Card. If playing as your Academic, play this card face up on any Voynichese Word in the Manuscript common pool unless otherwise specified by the text printed on your Academic card or any Voting Rules card in play. 
	 - You may propose an Alternate Manuscript language using a Language Card in your hand. This triggers a Scholarly Consensus Vote among all players with face-up Academic cards, according to the Voting Rules in play. Turn Gloss cards in the Manuscript common pool face down except those matching your proposed Manuscript Language. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card. 
	 - Propose a Crazy Idea Manuscript Language. You may also propose a novel suggestion for the Manuscript Language without playing a Language Card by spending 2 Backing chits.
	 - Propose a partial transliteration: Play a Glyph card on any Voynichese card in the Manuscript common pool. Follow the instructions of the text printed on the card. 
	 - Play a card that changes the Voting Rules. Follow the instructions in the text printed on the card. 
	 - Flip your Character / Academic Card to change the play of your turn.
	 - Spend 2 Backing chits to flip your Character / Academic Card and change the play at any time during your turn.
	 - Contribute to the Manuscript lore by playing legend cards according to the rules on the card.

If any other card is drawn, you must look through the deck and choose seven(or whatever the number of characters is) cards of your choosing and place them face down in front of you. Game objects, typically cards, have icons or other identifiers that identify them as belonging to specific categories. These tags may trigger special effects and/or have values and meaning that can vary, even within the scope of a single play. Tags are additional parameters on top of the base meaning of the game element, so tags represent a means of coupling the game element with more mechanisms and systems. Tags are also bookmarks that can reference a variable set of possible rules that are encoded elsewhere, so tags are also a means to modularize, or uncouple, game triggers and game effects.

In storytelling games, players are provided with conceptual, written, or pictorial stimuli which must be incorporated into a story of the players' creation. Once Upon a Time uses a selection of words while Rory's Story Cubes include ambiguous symbols. Some games like Snake Oil and Big Idea prompt players to pitch a product, which frequently takes the form of a brief story or vignette.

Other storytelling games include titles such as Tales of the Arabian Nights and Above and Below, game designs in which players don't create their own stories, but instead experience a story from the inside as one of the participants. Games along those lines might present players with a particular narrative situation, after which the player will make a choice that affects which end to the narrative is told — with the results of this narrative affecting the player's standing in the game.


= = = = = = = = = =
A game in which players are cooperating and competing with each other throughout the game, while trying to complete a common objective. To be classified as semi-cooperative, there must be two possible end states:

A) One or more (but unlikely to be all) players win
B) No players win

A game where players sometimes cooperate and sometimes compete but one always wins is not semi-cooperative. It is a Competitive game with a Negotiation mechanism.


= = = = = = = = = =
Secret unit deployment games are games that contain hidden information. Only the player controlling certain playing pieces has perfect information about the nature (or even the whereabouts) of those pieces. This mechanic is often used in wargames to simulate "fog of war".


= = = = = = = = = =
A game system that can be applied to a variety of different maps, starting resources and positions, and even different win and loss conditions. These variable conditions can be assembled into a broader narrative or campaign, or they can be entirely disconnected from one another.


= = = = = = = = = =
Some board games incorporate elements of role playing. It can be that players control a character that improves over time. It can also be a game that encourages or inspires Storytelling. This mechanic can be viewed as an extension of Variable Player Powers.

Resources are generated from a random process and distributed to qualifying players.


= = = = = = = = = =
Players ask and answer questions in a manner constrained by rules.

The Pieces themselves compose the Map.

This is distinct from Tile Placement in that the map elements remain “pieces” after placement, and accordingly continue to have agency in the game mechanics.

Pieces are removed from a structure, and play is affected by things that fall (as in Ker Plunk), or a complete collapse of the structure (as in Jenga).

Players possess one or more Action Tokens. Those who have an Action Token may take a turn, then they pass the token clockwise, allowing the next player to perform an action. Actions are performed in real time; - there is no pausing and structure within the turn.

Typically, to prevent stalling and to keep the game moving, in games with multiple Action Tokens, if both tokens are held by the same player, then they suffer a penalty.

Players have a special ability that they can use one time per game.

These may be unique to them, like 'feats' in Warmachine, or common to all players, like the special power chits in Finca.

Actions, resources, or resolution are shared between neighbors.

Rummy games have players placing combinations of cards or tiles on the table to score. Innovation is a good example of the Splaying side, where players can spread cards out to show particular sets of icons to empower abilities.

In some implementations the next play needs to be in a number range based on the last. For example, in L.L.A.M.A. the play must be the same or one higher than the last. In Spit, it must be one higher or lower.

Closed Drafting (or 'Card Drafting') is a means of distributing cards or other game elements to players through an ordered, closed selection process - typically "select and pass".

A typical implementation involves each player being dealt the same number of cards. Players then select one (or more) card(s) to keep, and pass the rest to their left. This continues until all cards are selected or discarded. 7 Wonders implements this type of draft.

An alternative is that only one player is dealt cards, and they take one and pass it until all players have cards. This obviously is strongly biased towards the first player, and needs to be supported thematically and balance-wise. Citadels implements this type of draft.

This is distinct from Open Drafting, with involves selection from a public display.

VOYNICH GAME

The base game should be fairly light weight and accessible, but the more you play, the more mysteries are revealed, which adds layers to gameplay, and build into a much heavier weight game, or at least, the option to play it as a more heavyweight game. 

TRANSLATION 
As various translation proposals for words build up, the Maniscript Pool will evolve into what could be a sensible phrase, or could be nonsense. In order to be a successful translation, a manuscript language proposal must 1) match a majority (but need not match all) of the proposed glosses 2) must be built of the glosses proposed by being played on the manuscript pool words, and 3) must successfully win a consensus vote according to the voting rules in play. 

THE WIN DECK
If the players successfully translate the manuscript, they get to play a win round. There is a special deck just for this round, which operates as a reveal about the true nature of the manuscript. The core set comes with “The Order’s Secret Waterworks” win deck. The final round is only played with one or two cards per player, thus the reveal is surprising and mysterious with each game play, and depending upon how the win deck cards interact, there may be variable solutions to the mystery. However, many other win decks could be purchased as expansions with very different win game scenarios. 
Maybe—End Game scenarios are one of two things: Either somebody proves the manuscript is a hoax or gibberish, in which case they win and that’s the end of the game, or players arrive at a successful translation, revealing the existence of the win deck (maybe the win deck is hidden in the packaging with a win deck rulebook and not advertised, so it’s a really surprising reveal. The clues must be pieced together to come to the conclusion that the win deck even exists. The win deck rulebook should strongly request that players keep its existence secret. Perhaps some of the cards in the win deck could have codes which provide a discount on expansion packs? 


Lots of personality — characters, and game itself
There are “stock characters” and generated characters (based on attribute card randomization / name randomizing / setting, etc)

Lots of mystery and intrigue, hidden secret cards and rules and mechanics and characters. Out-of-game mechanics and legacy game mechanics…players may get to keep certain cards to be playable in future games. 

Actually… that might be the core:
You’ve got the manuscript pool
And you’ve got the character pool
The character pool is the character you’re dealing with in that round… they can help or harm, depending on your choices 

Card categories should have very clear and intuitive iconography… Like portrait frames for characters, parchment backgrounds for words and manuscript related stuff, other book like backgrounds

Mapping the manuscript to language…
Scrabble tiles that go on the word cards
Some sort of limited dictionary’s of a few languages maybe?
A little bit about language phrenology and morphology?

And card sourcing
Get lists of language features

Constellations

Mabs
Kinds of castles
Medieval styles
Languages

We need Asian characters, New World characters

Royalls
